EWC's empirical Fisher is exactly the first-order form of this constraint when the preserved functional is each sample's loss. This derivation exposes a flaw: EWC implicitly weights each sample by the scale of its loss gradient, so well-fitted samples lose importance. EWC-DR observed this failure in classification; CLOC identifies its general cause. Improved Elastic Weight Consolidation (IEWC) penalizes output changes according to the first-order approximation of each old sample's loss level set, removing the weighting for any differentiable loss and output geometry, and prevents corrupt samples from dominating the importance matrix. Across classification, segmentation, language, forecasting, and diffusion, IEWC variants match or improve on EWC and outperform EWC-DR. In a held-out evaluation with validation-selected hyperparameters, uniform IEWC improves ImageNet-R accuracy over matched EWC by 2.00 percentage points (95% CI 0.93-3.07).

title: Privacy Leakage from Recurrent State in LLM Inference
author: Weimin Fu
Shikun Liu
Qiying Li
Yuntao Liu
Pan Li
Xiaolong Guo
abstract: Personalized LLM services place private facts and application instructions into a prompt, then retain representations of that context for later inference. Latent-state LLMs compress part of this history into fixed-size recurrent state. The information preserved by its learned updates is implicit, and later computation can expose it even when an observer receives neither the private text nor the responses. We investigate privacy leakage from recurrent state through partial-state probing and physical observation of its use. Our methodology separates recoverable information, persistence through public dialogue, causal influence on later decisions, and leakage through power. Experiments with released hybrid implementations show that a small state observation supports multiple predictions about private facts and response rules, and that personal attributes generalize to unseen authors. The information remains inferable after public dialogue and changes later decision margins. Complete-read power recovers private facts under a fixed execution schedule. On a partitioned GPU, an unprivileged account infers age from whole-device power during public requests; a separate state-isolation experiment establishes the recurrent contribution to this channel. These findings extend context confidentiality to the lifetime and execution of retained state. They identify access-control responsibilities for serving systems, telemetry restrictions for GPU operators, and data-dependent power leakage for accelerator designers.

title: Wayfinder: Adaptive Resource Routing from Agent Citations
author: Miguel Romero
George Karypis
abstract: To act effectively, agents must gather contextual information across resources such as chats, issue trackers, email and knowledge bases, to answer questions like "what was decided in the last project meeting?" or "where is the FAQ for our internal tooling?" Where this information lives in a user's environment is unknown to the agent, so it re-explores the same resources across consecutive interactions. Common routing approaches represent each resource as a tool and rely on high-level descriptions to generalize to unseen environments. Such descriptions often fail to separate similar or overlapping resources and cannot improve from the agent's subsequent interactions. We introduce Wayfinder, an adaptive router that uses the documents cited by the downstream agent as feedback about where relevant information resides. These citations update Wayfinder's internal resource representations, which subsequent interactions use to prioritize the resources likely to contain relevant information. We also introduce resource augmentation during offline reinforcement learning, which anonymizes and permutes resource identities to discourage training-time overfitting of which resource holds which topic; our ablations suggest it helps most when few training environments are available. Because no openly available professional environments pair realistic queries with resource-access patterns, we construct and release three controlled testbeds derived from existing datasets: NFCorpus, FEVER and Tech Startup. Compared with supervised, tool-retrieval and contextual bandit baselines under a shared closed-loop protocol, Wayfinder gives the best routing when resources contain semantically overlapping content that static descriptions cannot distinguish, while description-based tool retrieval suffices when resources are drawn from distinct corpora.

title: Sub-actions in Action: Text-Guided Hand-Role Alignment for Sub-Action Recognition
author: Sadegh Rahmaniboldaji
Filip Rybansky
Quoc Vuong
Frank Guerin
Andrew Gilbert
abstract: Our objective is to enhance VLMs ability to distinguish the roles of the left and right hands in egocentric actions. We introduce sub-action detection, a task that requires models to explicitly recognise the left- and right-hand roles and their manipulated objects within an ongoing high-level action. To address this challenge, we propose BiScopeNet, a framework that augments existing video-LLMs without modifying their vision encoders or language models. BiScopeNet incorporates two components: FocusAlign, a gated text-guided attention-based module that selectively aligns video features with textual context to emphasise action-relevant cues, and MetaLoss, a masked, object-weighted loss that prioritises visually grounded terms. To supervise sub-action detection, we introduce BiScopeCap-100K, a large-scale video-level dataset curated from existing egocentric datasets, providing dense captions that jointly describe high-level actions, left/right-hand roles, and manipulated objects, enriched with spatial metadata for grounding. Across the evaluated Video-LLM backbones, BiScopeNet improves action, hand-role, and object recognition over the corresponding supervised baselines, achieving the strongest aggregate performance among the evaluated configurations on BiScopeCap.

title: Pothole Risk Assessment with Geometrically Grounded Vision Language Models
author: Abdalmalek Aburaddaha
Zaid A. El Shair
Ali Al-Bustami
Samir A. Rawashdeh
abstract: Potholes impose billions of dollars in annual vehicle damage, yet detectors report only where potholes are, not how severe they are or what to do. Judging severity from a single RGB image is ill-posed, and ungrounded vision-language model (VLM) assessments tend to be over-conservative. We present a five-stage modular framework for the offline assessment of already-detected potholes that combines geometric measurements with VLM reasoning: perspective transformation, zero-shot SAM segmentation, geometric feature extraction, Gemini 2.5 Pro severity classification with composite risk scoring, and natural-language warning generation. We evaluate it on 3,092 potholes in 1,119 dashcam scenes against independent references. Severity agreement with a prediction-free three-annotator panel is weak (Cohen's $\kappa = 0.139$, 95% CI [0.00, 0.28]; $n = 101$) and far below the annotators' agreement with one another ($\kappa = 0.605$); against physically measured depth on an independent RGB-D dataset, it is also weak ($\kappa = 0.098$), although the predicted classes preserve the order of measured depths. The severity classes are therefore perceived visual categories, not depth measurements. Geometric grounding does change the warnings: relative to an image-only baseline, it moves 26.7% of scenes out of the high-urgency tier and raises critical-tier assignments by 109% (Stuart-Maxwell $p < 10^{-15}$), and in a blind study, three raters preferred the grounded warnings 3.5:1. A six-arm prompt ablation attributes the hybrid prompt's rule adherence to the per-pothole measurements rather than to the rubric or worked examples. At USD 0.105 per scene, it suits large-scale offline infrastructure assessment; its maneuver suggestions are advisory research outputs, not validated vehicle guidance.

title: Vocabulary-Free Next-Event Prediction on Temporal Graphs
author: Zhishang Luo
Venu Madhav Tammali
Amila Weerasinghe
Osso Vahabzadeh
Olcay Boz
Xue Hao
Yusu Wang
abstract: Autoregressive transformer training through next-token prediction has driven remarkable advances in language modeling and has become increasingly effective for time-series modeling. Yet its success in temporal graph learning remains limited, and most temporal link-prediction methods are discriminative rather than autoregressive. While temporal graphs can have a natural serialization through chronological ordering edges, they lack an obvious graph-independent tokenization: existing node tokenization often uses a vocabulary that grows with the number of nodes, limiting scalability and cross-graph training. We propose GTGT, Generative Temporal Graph Transformer, a simple yet powerful vocabulary-free framework for self-supervised next-event prediction on temporal graphs. It predicts events for observed destinations, behavioral descriptors for novel destinations, and time gaps before new event. These targets have shared meanings across graphs, allowing one transformer to train across disjoint node sets without node-specific learned parameters. Local node identifiers let attention capture graph structure: Theoretically, we can show that our transformer-based model has the capacity for time-respecting message passing mechanisms. On Temporal Graph Benchmark (TGB), our GTGT not only achieves comparable or better link-prediction performance than established baselines, but also has much lower training cost. These results open the door to temporal graph pretraining for forecasting and other downstream tasks, providing a concrete step toward temporal graph foundation models.

title: "It's Just a Small Weapon": What Rewarding Misbehavior During RL Does to Character-Trained Models
author: Mohammad Omar Khursheed
Thomas Morris
Fabien Roger
abstract: Developers train models to follow a consistent character using methods like Model Spec Midtraining (Li et al., 2026), which have been hypothesized to make alignment more robust and generalize broadly. However, it is possible for subsequent RL with misspecified rewards to work against character training. In this work, we apply character training to teach gpt-oss-20b a semi-realistic constitution and study how it interacts with two types of RL that reward breaking the constitution's rules (opposing RL): answering harmful requests rewritten as math problems, and reward hacking in agentic coding environments. The character-trained models learn both behaviors easily, though they are slightly slower than gpt-oss-20b to answer harmful requests. Character-trained models also display more motivated reasoning on harmful answers than gpt-oss-20b, and hack on some tasks which monitors find harder to catch. Finally, since explaining the reasons behind rules can improve how alignment generalizes (Kutasov et al., 2026), we compare constitutions that justify the same rules by grounding them in a value or not, and find little difference between motivations on misalignment, honesty, and capability evaluations.

title: KVPath: Connecting Key-Value Representations Across Transformer Layers
author: Xuan Luo
Zhiyuan Wang
Hanzhong Cao
Xifeng Yan
abstract: Transformers typically cache an independent key-value (KV) representation for each token at every layer. Recent work reveals that a token's KV representations across neighboring layers are correlated and contain shared information. We hypothesize that this correlation implies incremental inter-layer changes, which can be effectively captured by low-dimensional deltas. Motivated by this, we propose KVPath, a new KV representation paradigm that connects KV representations across the network depth into a path. The path establishes a full-dimensional base KV at the first layer, while subsequent layers generate low-dimensional delta KVs to update the preceding KV, thereby constructing their own KV states. By caching the base KV once alongside these compact delta KVs, KVPath preserves distinct layer-specific representations without storing full KV states at every layer. We develop two variants of KVPath: KVPath-Residual, which updates vector values via residual addition, and KVPath-Rolling, which progressively updates feature dimensions in a rolling manner. Under matched parameter counts, KVPath reduces KV-cache storage by up to 68\% for Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) and 55\% for Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), while maintaining or even improving model performance.

title: One Future Fits All: Text-to-image AI and the Narrowing of Global Imagination
author: Stephanie Diepeveen
Somnath Batabyal
Edward Ademolu
Peter Chonka
Gabriele de Seta
Iginio Gagliardone
Elisabeth Gunawan
Fabio Gygi
Yidnekachew Haile
Yenn Lee
Chipo Mapondera
Craig Ryder
Matti Pohjonen
Michiel Baas
abstract: Persistence of algorithmic bias is well established in scholarship, reflecting, reproducing and reshaping inequalities and injustices. Yet, as technology changes, we cannot assume that inequalities will be reproduced in the same or similar forms. This article explores the reproduction of bias in text-to-image generative AI, looking at the tool, Microsoft Bing Create, based on DALL E 3. It draws on results of a collaborative exploratory study of 907 image-based outputs of text-to-image generation in 15 languages and concerning 12 countries. We utilise the notion of synthetic probes (de Seta, 2024) to iteratively explore correlations of inputs and outputs within the context of place, language and power. We find striking simplicity in the scope of possibilities through which Bing Create considers the current and future city. Stripping out (explicit) indications of conflict, poverty and politics, we are left with images whose localised diversity harkens back to versions of Orientalist imaginaries. Images of the future emerge as one civilising mission or modernisation narrative, with all places headed to one future of hovercrafts, urban gardens and solar panels, encased in a composition of shades of blue and green. We argue that the visual outputs of this generative AI tool reflect and reproduce a simple but pervasive and persistent colonial/developmental worldview. We explore explanations for this emergent narrative and its implications, suggesting the threat of generative AI is not in its complexity or intelligence, but rather its banality. With this, we propose banality not as mere repetition, but the systematic narrowing of representational possibility: a convergence on tourist-friendly, depoliticised, development-saturated visual grammars that smooth contradiction and foreclose plural futurisms.

title: Measuring Preferred Representation in AI-generated Images with Community Scorers
author: Melanie F. Pradier
Camilla Longden
Anja Thieme
Rita F. Marques
Nari Johnson
Sidhika Balachandar
Xinnuo Xu
Linda Y. Wen
Martin Grayson
Katja Hofmann
Cecily Morrison
Daniela Massiceti
abstract: AI-generated images often misrepresent historically marginalised communities, with real-world consequences beyond the images themselves. However, conventional metrics fail to measure how communities want to be represented in AI-generated images. To address this, we introduce the concept of preferred representation. Building on previous work, we propose a measurement instrument that operationalises this concept through a Community Scorer - a model that evaluates a specific community's preferred representation in AI-generated images. We interrogate the validity of Community Scorers on three diverse disability communities that span the Global North and South. The results show that Community Scorers align significantly better with community ratings compared to other widely used text-to-image metrics. We then demonstrate the usefulness of these scorers in a downstream content filtering task. We release the Community Preference Dataset to enable others to optimise how Community Scorers can be scaled for culturally specific evaluation of AI-generated visual media.

title: A Matching Lower Bound for Online Smooth Calibration
author: Kaixuan Ji
Quanquan Gu
abstract: We study smooth calibration error in sequential binary prediction, which measures how far a sequence of probabilistic forecasts is from being calibrated and, unlike the classical expected calibration error, is robust to small perturbations of the forecasts. Against adaptive adversaries, the minimax smooth calibration error is known to lie between $\Omega(T^{1/3})$ and $O(\sqrt{T})$ (Qiao and Zheng, 2024), where $T$ is the number of rounds. In this paper, we close this gap by constructing a new adversary whose outcome mean moves with the forecaster's cumulative residual. This design makes compensating for past residuals costly, and forces every forecaster to incur an expected smooth calibration error of $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$. This lower bound matches the known upper bound up to universal constants, and further implies $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ lower bounds for calibration distance and lower calibration distance. Overall, our results settle the minimax rates of these calibration measures in sequential prediction. The proof ideas are partially developed by GPT-6 Astra under the authors' guidance.

title: Show Your Work in Swahili: Reinforcement Learning for Native-Language Mathematical Reasoning
author: Jessica Lundin
Katherine Rosenfeld
David Adelani
Geoffrey Mosoti Nyakiongora
Halfan Ngowo
Sloan Coffin
Ralph Abboud
Guillaume Chabot-Couture
abstract: We present Fikiria, a two-stage SFT+GRPO recipe for Swahili mathematical reasoning. Its reward multiplies a format gate by a weighted sum of answer accuracy and the ChrF\texttt{++} similarity of the Swahili reasoning to an in-language reference chain of thought, so that training targets the surface fidelity of the reasoning trace and not only the final answer. We train on a 2.3k-problem Swahili dataset created by translating GSM8K with GPT-4.1 and filtering with SSA-COMET. On AfriMGSM Swahili, Fikiria-AfriqueQwen-14B reaches 79.2\%. Under the same fixed prompt and strict answer-format scoring, GPT-4o reaches 68.0\%, partly because it often fails the required answer format; IrokoBench reports 78.8\% for GPT-4o using a best-per-model prompt, a figure numerically close to ours but not directly comparable. In a small human evaluation with co-author annotators, GPT-4o's outputs were preferred overall. ChrF\texttt{++} measures surface fidelity, not the validity of individual reasoning steps.

title: How Do People Debug Complex SQL Queries With LLMs? A Qualitative Study
author: Nicole Sullivan
Ella Cao
Leilani Battle
Magdalena Balazinska
abstract: While LLMs are increasingly used in various contexts, we lack a fundamental understanding of how they impact SQL query debugging. In response, we conducted a user study with 16 participants of varying SQL expertise, examining how they debug complex SQL queries with and without LLM support. Initial benchmarking indicated that our selected models are already capable SQL debuggers. Qualitative analyses of our study data revealed that while participants trusted the LLM, they varied widely in how and whether they delegated debugging tasks to the LLMs, which we characterized through a new three-state model of participants' SQL reasoning processes. Additionally, participants enforced specific collaborative roles for the LLM such as TA or sounding board, which participants controlled by withholding context from the LLM. These findings suggest that LLM-based tools could enable preset role selection, broader context management, and flexible automation features, including low automation options, to support SQL debugging moving forward.

title: ADAPT: Agentic Diff-Aware Patch Testing for Pull Requests
author: Vahid Haratian
Atakan Akar
Eray TÃ¼zÃ¼n
abstract:
Modern software development relies on pull requests (PRs) that introduce small, targeted code changes. Once merged, these changes should be protected by focused tests that exercise the behavior the PR introduces, yet developers often submit PRs without such tests, leaving the new behavior unguarded against future regressions. Most test generation techniques target entire software units and optimize objectives such as code coverage rather than the behavior a change introduces, and prior diff-aware approaches have had limited success in capturing it.
We propose ADAPT (Agentic Diff-Aware Patch Testing), a regression test generation approach that uses an autonomous coding agent to produce change-focused tests for PRs. Given a PR, the agent analyzes the diff between the base and head versions to identify the modified functions and their context, then plans and generates candidate unit tests. A dedicated fail-to-pass (F2P) verification tool runs each candidate on both versions and, after F2P success, reports which executable changed lines remain uncovered; guided by this feedback, the agent iteratively refines its tests.
We evaluate ADAPT on the same 426 real-world PRs used by the prior state-of-the-art baseline, with GPT-4o and GPT-5-mini. ADAPT+GPT-4o reaches an F2P rate of 62.0% (264/426), compared with BLAST's reported 35.4% (151/426), while ADAPT+GPT-5-mini reaches 89.9% (383/426). On 137 PRs shared with Change And Cover (ChaCo), ADAPT achieves full patch coverage on 83.9% of PRs, compared with 79.6% for ChaCo, at considerably lower time and cost. A manual evaluation confirms that the F2P-valid tests target each PR's intended change, with mean scores of up to 4.54/5 for importance, 4.35/5 for assertion strength, and 4.49/5 for readability, often covering behavior beyond the developer-written tests.

title: Robo-SWE: An Executable Issue-Resolution Dataset Mined from Robot Software Repositories
author: Vahid Haratian
Vahid Ansari
Mohammadhossein Malmir
Alois Knoll
abstract: Coding agents are evaluated mostly on general-purpose software, but domain-specific systems require domain-aware evaluation. Robot software is a particularly challenging case: Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) packages have their own build tools, simulators and learning frameworks are built on physics engines, and behavior that depends on timing and hardware is hard to test. We present Robo-SWE, a dataset of 236 executable issue-resolution tasks mined from merged pull requests in 28 public robotics repositories in four domains: ROS 2 systems, simulation and physics engines, robotics algorithm libraries, and robot-learning frameworks. Each task contains the original issue text, a container recipe for the repository at the commit before the fix, the developers' fix, and the developers' tests, which fail before the fix and pass after it in repeated offline runs. The dataset also keeps a provenance ledger of all 1,567 candidate pull requests, with the stage each reached and the reason for every rejection, and, as a first use, 3,540 graded attempts by five coding-agent setups with recorded patches and 3,529 available trajectories. Across three runs per primary setup, resolve rates range from 45.8% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 to 56.5% for Claude Opus 5.5; GPT-6.1 Sol reaches 54.1% at maximum effort and 52.5% at medium effort, and GPT-6 Astra 51.4%. GLM-5.3 resolves 46.2%, and Kimi K3.1 Pro 43.9%. The tasks are validated by execution; verification of their fairness by human reviewers is future work. The dataset and public leaderboard are available online.

title: Intent-Aware Protection for AI Agents
author: Fady Copty
Neta Haiby
Max Braitmaiere
Julia Korsunsky
abstract: AI agents increasingly access enterprise data, invoke powerful tools, and act with limited human oversight. Existing security defenses primarily detect prompt injection, harmful outputs, or suspicious behavior, but do not determine whether an agent remains faithful to the purpose for which it was deployed. An action may contain no attack pattern and stay within granted permissions while still violating the agent's role, organizational constraints, or purpose. We introduce Intent- Aware Security, a framework that treats trusted agent intent as a first-class security object. We define Intent Preservation and Intent Drift, and operationalize them through an Intent Profile: an agent-specific representation extracted from organizational, role, and developer intent. We further introduce an Intent-Aware benchmark of 887 validated samples across 35 agents, built by a generation procedure that fixes ground-truth labels before LLM realization, and four Intent Profile-based protections: pre-execution detection, post-execution detection, input alignment, and system-prompt hardening. Across all evaluations, Intent Profile-based protection outperforms all profile-free baselines on the primary metric. On our benchmark, it raises four-class acro-F1 from 45% to 79% (Out-of-Scope F1 from 8% to 76%). On more than 10,000 executed AgentDojo trajectories, where ground truth comes from environment state, profile-based post-execution detection reaches 0.949 AUROC versus AlignmentCheck 0.909, 0.897 with raw agent configuration and 0.843 without context. Profile-based input alignment improves protection success by 7 points over DataFilter with a comparable benign utility. These results suggest that an agent's intended purpose can serve as a useful security reference for detecting and mitigating deviations from its deployed role and operational boundaries.

title: SwarmSafe-Delta: Isolating Message Effects on LLM Agent Safety
author: Junru Zhu
abstract:
When a tool-using LLM agent team violates policy, aggregate outcomes do not reveal whether an upstream message changed the executor's action. We introduce SwarmSafe-Delta, a paired executable protocol that freezes upstream computation, varies real, hidden, and format-matched placebo delivery, and scores a single committed action against deterministic benign and risky policy states under preassigned budgets.
Across four models and constructed optional tasks, real delivery at $N=4$ produces 21.4% risky-world violations, versus 5.0% with placebo and 1.0% with hidden delivery (paired differences +16.4 and +20.3 percentage points). Real delivery also improves benign task success, illustrating that suppressing communication sacrifices utility. In a second regime constructed to require an upstream lookup route, real delivery improves safe completion by 74.2 points relative to hidden delivery. These effects quantify message-delivery contrasts under specified information dependencies, not naturally occurring failure rates.
Exploratory action-level analyses show that the effect depends strongly on whether the upstream message recommends a prerequisite check or direct execution; model differences also largely track these message compositions. The contribution is a controlled, execution-grounded measurement protocol rather than a general claim that agent communication is harmful or protective.

title: Temporal Context-Aware Spam Detection Using Transformer-Based NLP Models
author: Fariz Zeynalov
Razim Mammadli
abstract: Spam detection is usually treated as single-message classification, ignoring behavioral patterns that emerge across sequences of messages from the same sender. We study outbound SMS spam detection at the carrier level, where the goal is to predict at send time whether a carrier will flag a message as spam. Using a proprietary production database of 43,741 outbound SMS messages with UTC transmission timestamps and carrier delivery statuses, we report three sets of results. On an 8,749-message held-out test set, a TF-IDF + logistic regression baseline reaches AUC-ROC 0.8721, and a text-only DeBERTa-v3-base classifier reaches AUC-ROC 0.9011 and F1 0.8412. A deployed DistilBERT model augmented with inter-message temporal features reaches accuracy 0.8238, spam-class F1 0.8382, and recall 0.9128 at threshold 0.5 on a separate, class-balanced 20,000-message production evaluation set; these results are not directly comparable with the held-out test results. We also describe TemporalBertSpam, an architecture that encodes each sender's message history with a causal Transformer, and outline the same-split evaluation needed to measure its contribution.

title: Does a Self-Learning Migration Agent Learn? An Audited Evaluation of Evidence-Graded Experience Memory for Oracle-to-PostgreSQL Migration
author: Oleg Grynets
Vasyl Lyashkevych
Valeriia Oliferuk
Vladyslav Babenko
Danylo Kovalchuk
Dmytro Kostetskyi
abstract: Do large language model (LLM) migration agents learn from accumulated experience, or do apparent gains reflect retrieval and reference reuse? We evaluate an evidence-graded agent for Oracle-to-PostgreSQL migration across four studies. On 1,833 documentation-derived source-reference pairs, persistent memory improved reference conformity (RC) over a no-memory baseline by 0.015 [0.004, 0.025], while policy adaptation added no gain (-0.004 [-0.010, 0.001]). An audit found that 264 of 367 held-out units (72%) shared a PostgreSQL reference with training, and the memory effect on the 103 leak-free units fell to 0.002 [-0.008, 0.011]. A model-free nearest-target copy baseline scored RC 0.222, outperforming all LLM systems (at most 0.163). A reference-grouped split reduced copying to 0.119; a rerun on 374 units in 118 independent target groups found no statistically distinguishable memory effect (0.005 [-0.003, 0.017]) and no policy effect. A separate Oracle-grounded evaluation on 216-224 real PL/SQL units showed that 10-22% of PostgreSQL-accepted units were behaviorally incorrect; a human-gated fix cycle increased demonstrably correct units from 98/216 to 167/224. A write-back study showed a 54% decline in retrieval margin as the knowledge base grew from 12 to 1,200 entries. We derive six evaluation rules that distinguish cross-task learning from reference leakage, copying, metric artifacts, and unstable feedback.

title: HyperPage: Learned Page Layouts for Disk-Resident Graph Vector Indexes
author: Xinyu Zhang
Jingze Li
Baihua Zheng
Weiwei Sun
abstract: Disk-resident graph indexes such as DiskANN store each vector with its graph edges as one record on SSD pages. A search needs the page of every record it expands, so its page reads depend on the page layout, that is, which records share a page. Search agents trained with reinforcement learning query one such index run after run, and every graph traversal can be logged with the records it expands. We therefore use the logs of a finished run to lay out the index for a declared memory budget, so later runs read fewer pages. In contrast, existing layouts such as Starling and MARGO are computed from the graph and vectors and use no logs. Learning a layout from logs is challenging, because the logs must stay valid under every layout, the saving depends on what the budget caches, and the best layout is NP-hard to find. Our key observation is that DiskANN-style search routes on in-memory codes and the records it expands, never on their page-mates. As a result, the logged traversals price every layout by replay, and cached records add no page reads. Accordingly, we propose HyperPage, which first builds layouts for the declared budget on the logged traversals of uncached records. It then selects one layout, together with the budget split between hot records and a page cache, by replaying validation steps. In addition, a Lagrangian lower bound shows how far a layout may be from the optimum. We learn from one Search-R1 agent run and test on a later run with a different reward, over 1M and 21M passages. Across seven cache budgets, HyperPage reads 5.2% to 21.2% fewer pages than MARGO, and no compared layout reads fewer. The advantage is largest when the cache is small. For example, at 1% of the 1M index, MARGO needs nearly 3 times the budget to read as few pages. On the 21M index, HyperPage also cuts search time per step by up to 10.4%. The saving holds for a second agent model and a second corpus.

title: Fault Injection Attacks on Q-Learning: Analysis, Vulnerabilities, and Countermeasures
author: Tom Slooff
Anthony Etim
Jiaqi Yu
Francesco Regazzoni
Jakub Szefer
abstract: Hardware fault injection attacks threaten machine learning systems, yet their impact on reinforcement learning (RL) has received little attention despite the use of RL in safety-critical applications. This paper presents a security analysis of Q-Learning implementations under voltage and clock glitching attacks on a ChipWhisperer platform, evaluating five variants: Standard, Robust, Resilient, Linear, and Deep Q-Learning. In standard Q-Table implementations, faults corrupt reward computation, action selection, and Q-value updates during learning, and change the selected action during inference. Robust Q-Learning does not prevent these attacks: NaN and infinite values injected during learning persist in the Q-table, and its greedy policy uses the same code as standard Q-Learning. This paper also evaluates a Resilient Q-Learning variant that applies triple modular redundancy with majority voting. It corrects corruption of a single Q-table copy, but inputs shared by the copies, such as the reward, and the voting code itself remain outside its protection. The analysis extends to Linear and Deep Q-Learning, where faults corrupt stored weights during learning and change actions during inference. Moving beyond benchmark environments, this work evaluates an online traffic light controller in a microscopic traffic simulator, where a single injected infinite value degrades accumulated vehicle waiting time by 148x while corrupting under 4% of the Q-table, and where triple modular redundancy corrected the faults injected in our tests, although glitching could still halt the device. Altogether, this work provides a basis for understanding and securing RL deployments against fault injection attacks.

title: PolicySniff: Inferring Agent Policy States through Shared-GPU Execution
author: Weimin Fu
Minghao Shao
Zeng Wang
Qiying Li
Yuntao Liu
Johann Knechtel
Ozgur Sinanoglu
Muhammad Shafique
Ramesh Karri
Xiaolong Guo
abstract: LLM agents apply approval settings, such as whether to ask before a consequential tool call, through instructions in their system prompt, and operators keep these settings confidential by restricting access to prompts and responses. Audits check whether an agent obeys its setting, not whether a neighboring process can infer which setting is deployed. PolicySniff infers an agent's approval-policy state through shared-GPU execution. A co-resident attacker that knows the candidate settings and the task first profiles both settings, then times only its own GPU kernels while the agent processes the task. The policy prefix is cached before capture, so the attacker observes processing of a task suffix that is identical under both settings. On an eager sparse mixture-of-experts runtime, where each selected expert runs as separate work, a frozen and blinded study identified the deployed setting at 94.17% balanced accuracy on its primary estimand. Across all authorization conditions, accuracy was 88.82% on tasks for which both settings produce the same decision and 91.98% on tasks where they differ. Hardware replays of expert routing show that its temporal density and layer-and-bucket alignment carry the policy information. Behavioral compliance does not imply configuration confidentiality: deployments that keep their approval setting private should measure its distinguishability on the serving runtime and enforce authorization outside the model.

title: JudgeMix: Judge-Guided Mixed-Rollout Data Synthesis for LLM Agents
author: Cheng-Yu Hsieh
Ting-Yao Hu
Sanjoy Chowdhury
Oncel Tuzel
Raviteja Vemulapalli
abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories is a standard paradigm for training LLM agents. However, it suffers from a well-known training-inference distribution mismatch, calling for target-aware data synthesis strategies that ground the training data in the target model's native state distribution. To bridge this gap, emerging approaches incorporate the expert either to guide mixed rollouts alongside the target model, or to provide dense step-wise supervision. Nonetheless, existing methods apply expert assistance blind to the target model's inherent behavior: they either disrupt the rollout using sub-optimal random intervention heuristics, or they enforce indiscriminate uniform supervision that unnecessarily overwrites the model's already-correct actions. We introduce JudgeMix, a judge-guided data synthesis framework that dynamically interleaves the target model and expert based on step-wise semantic evaluations. JudgeMix queries expert guidance precisely when the target model struggles, ensuring high trajectory success rates while keeping the state distribution aligned with the target model. It additionally uses the judge evaluation to reweight expert supervision on different steps, preserving model's inherent valid behavior while correcting its errors. On two agentic tool-use benchmarks, AppWorld and AutomationBench, JudgeMix demonstrates consistent superior performance to existing methods, with improvements up to 10 pass@1 points.

title: Stack more levels: how to get general and human-like Mario playing
author: Shinichi Arimura
Yuchen Li
Julian Togelius
abstract: Super Mario Bros. is widely used in game AI and procedural content generation (PCG), yet it remains unclear whether a model-free agent can reliably win unseen levels. To address this question, we train Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agents on increasingly large sets of PCG-generated Mario levels and evaluate their generalization on 1000 held-out test levels. We then shape competent PPO policies into three gameplay archetypes---runner, killer, and collector. Finally, we fine-tune these PPO policies using Diffusion-Reward Adversarial Imitation Learning (DRAIL) with human gameplay demonstrations. We find that increasing the number of distinct PCG-generated training levels generally improves unseen-level performance, and that fine-tuning PPO policies with DRAIL increases action-level human-likeness while preserving much of the persona induced by PPO pretraining.

title: Fast Serverless LLM Cold Starts by Sharing and Prewarming Startup Work
author: Hongjin Kim
Igjae Kim
Kwanghoon Choi
Minho Ha
Jaehyuk Huh
abstract: When a serverless LLM platform launches a model worker on demand, the cold start lasts roughly a minute, yet only 5-11% of it is spent loading weights. Most of the remainder goes to compilation, memory profiling and runtime setup, which each server performs again even though the outcome is identical across servers or independent of the model. We present Cairn. The server that is first to start a model publishes the weights and engine artifacts to a CXL memory pool shared across the cluster, and the remaining servers read them in place. Model-independent setup is completed ahead of time inside warm containers, and a template process replaces each container as soon as it is used. With ServerlessLLM on vLLM v0.20, six models from 1B to 14B, and two servers that share an emulated CXL pool, Cairn speeds up cold starts by 4.1-5.2x on servers without a checkpoint of their own and reduces median TTFT on a request stream by 64%.

title: Data-Efficient LLM Safety Alignment Guided by Interpretable Features
author: Hongyu Li
Zhan Yu
Zhe Zhao
Kimmo Yan
Xiong Kuang
Renfen Hu
abstract: Existing large language models typically rely on massive fine-tuning datasets for safety alignment, which results in higher costs for safety alignment and often leads to the problem of over-refusal. We propose Less is Safer (LIS), a compact yet highly effective dataset for safety alignment, constructed through interpretable feature-guided selection and adversarial synthesis. Specifically, we leverage Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) activations to efficiently select prompts that cover diverse and interpretable safety features. Then, we employ a multi-agent adversarial synthesis framework to generate harmless prompts that nevertheless elicit unnecessary refusals. LIS contains only 2.4K samples, yet outperforms much larger datasets, e.g., TRIDENT-Core (26K), TRIDENT-Edge (19K) and WildJailbreak (262K), in overall performance on four safety and five over-refusal benchmarks. Through ablation experiments, we demonstrate that neither safety data nor over-refusal data alone can achieve optimal results. We also used safety features from SAE, annotated by an LLM, for data filtering, but the results were inferior to those obtained using the pipeline proposed in this paper.

title: PERA: Plug-in Experts for Robotic Actions in Continual Whole-Body Control
author: Shangchao Hu
Yadan Sun
Xibo Yu
Wei Huang
abstract: Motion imitation enables humanoid robots to acquire whole-body skills such as walking and dancing. However, fine-tuning an entire policy for a new skill can affect existing behaviors, while training a separate policy for each skill increases training and maintenance costs. We present PERA, a method for learning new skills by reusing existing motion capabilities. PERA freezes a pretrained mixture-of-experts policy and trains an additional task expert and its routing score using task rewards or teacher-action supervision. In Unitree G1 simulation, each added task module contains approximately 1.03% of the parameters of the base actor. Built on our pretrained policy, PERA successfully completes all ten new tasks. Disabling the expert restores the original computation path of the base policy, which still fully executes all 126 original motions. Enabling the expert also improves the execution of some dance motions not used to train that expert, indicating that its benefits extend beyond its training motions. Experiments with HoloMotion further demonstrate the applicability of PERA to different base policies.

title: SBA: A Practical Memory Performance Denial-of-Service Attack
author: Amin Mamandipoor
Connor Rudy Sullivan
Cole Ridge Strickler
Mohammad Alian
Heechul Yun
abstract:
Modern cloud platforms use memory bandwidth regulation to isolate co-located workloads, implicitly assuming that high aggregate bandwidth consumption implies high interference. We show that this assumption is fundamentally flawed.
We present the Single-Bank Attack (SBA), a practical memory denial-of-service attack that induces extreme cross-core slowdowns---over three orders of magnitude on memory-intensive victims (e.g., LLM decode)---while consuming less than 1 GB/s of memory bandwidth. SBA exploits the gap between peak and worst-case DRAM throughput by concentrating memory write operations on a single bank, forcing persistent row conflicts and frequent write draining, thereby collapsing the memory service rate. Across Intel and AMD systems, including DDR5- and HBM2E-based platforms, SBA consistently causes orders-of-magnitude slowdowns under realistic multi-tenant settings, revealing a fundamental limitation of bandwidth-centric memory isolation.
We further show that this localized contention propagates system-wide: single-bank congestion saturates memory controller queues and induces back-pressure into shared cache and coherence structures, ultimately throttling memory request injection across cores. Consequently, severe interference can arise even at low aggregate bandwidth, evading existing bandwidth-based QoS mechanisms such as Intel RDT MBA.
To address this limitation, we propose IQ-MemGuard, a lightweight, software-based memory bandwidth regulator that detects sustained contention using microarchitectural signals and selectively throttles pathological request injection. Our implementation on an Intel platform effectively mitigates SBA, whereas Intel's hardware QoS mechanism fails completely.

title: An Extensive Evaluation of Machine Learning and Deep Learning Approaches for Sentiment Analysis: Insights from Amazon Customer Reviews
author: Muhammed Ihsan Corak
Cuiyuan Wang
Xiaowen Zhang
abstract: The rapid growth of user-generated text on online platforms creates opportunities for understanding customer opinion and supporting data-driven decisions. This study compares five traditional machine learning classifiers (Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Bernoulli Naive Bayes, Linear Support Vector Classifier, and Multinomial Naive Bayes) and six deep learning architectures (LSTM, Bi-LSTM, GRU, RNN, Attention, and FastText) for three-class sentiment classification of 568,454 Amazon Fine Food Reviews. Machine learning models used Bag-of-Words (BoW) and TF-IDF features limited to 5,000 terms; deep learning models used learned embeddings over a 20,000-word vocabulary. Models were evaluated on the original imbalanced data and on a random-oversampled balanced set of 1,070,469 reviews, using accuracy, macro and per-class precision, recall, and F1-score, and training time. On the balanced set, Random Forest with BoW achieved 99\% accuracy and the Attention model achieved 98.7\%. Linear SVC reached 89\% accuracy in 1 min 15 s, and Logistic Regression reached 90\% in 3 min 37 s. On the imbalanced set, the Attention model achieved 97.8\% accuracy, and FastText achieved 95.3\% in 3 min 26 s, while the RNN reached 91.9\% with a neutral-class F1-score of 0.08. Deep learning models were more stable across class distributions, whereas the best classical model depended on balancing. We also report a user-facing application that applies the trained Random Forest and Attention models to new review text. Because the labels are derived from star ratings, the results measure agreement with rating-derived sentiment classes rather than annotated sentiment; the dataset is a single source, and the findings should be read with that limitation in mind.

title: An Agentic Python Framework for LLM-Driven UVM Testbench Synthesis with Closed-Loop Compiler Feedback
author: Vikash Kumar
abstract: Protocol bridge verification is a persistent bottleneck in SoC development: for every new bridge instance, engineers hand-craft a full UVM testbench from scratch, consuming 40--100 engineering hours of bring-up effort. We present an agentic Python framework that generates complete, protocol-aware UVM testbenches for arbitrary IP and subsystem configurations from a structured Verification Manifest---a JSON specification encoding interface topology, protocol semantics, and coverage intent. The framework employs a dual closed-loop architecture: an inner compiler feedback loop that injects categorised UVM diagnostics rather than raw tool output, and an outer coverage loop driven by intent-gap analysis against the Manifest. Validated on the AMBA AHB-to-APB bridge---a representative production protocol bridge with a 7-state control FSM, two-phase APB handshake, and non-trivial burst serialisation logic---the framework achieves 96.8% functional coverage, a $4.7\times$ bring-up speedup, and a Protocol Verification Completeness score of 0.87, with only 2.1% of the generated 4,623-line testbench requiring human correction. The generated scoreboard independently identified a critical RTL functional fault that the manual baseline missed entirely. Generalisation across four protocol families confirms that speedup increases with protocol complexity, ranging from $3.1\times$ (APB Subordinate) to $6.1\times$ (CHI Subordinate).

title: Turning Multi-Agent Communication into Token-Level Credit with On Policy Self Distillation
author: Zixu Wang
Yu Zhao
Xing Zheng
Bingbing Xu
Tian Xueyun
JiaTang Luo
Weiqiang Wang
Bowen Song
Huawei Shen
Xueqi Cheng
abstract: Reinforcement learning improves problem solving in large language model multi-agent systems. Existing approaches overlook communication knowledge or compress it into scalar rewards, leaving coarse credit with little guidance on which decisions each agent should reinforce or revise. OPSD4MAS converts future communication into fine-grained token-level credit through On Policy Self Distillation (OPSD). An external model extracts facts and assesses their trajectory relations for coarse-grained filtering, followed by fine-grained leave-one-out filtering of target-token influence against agent-wise outcome advantages. The fact-conditioned policy supplies token-level credit, combined with GRPO through a linearly annealed joint objective. Our method improves mathematical pass@4 over GRPO by up to 20.00 percentage points. Ablations support complete filtering, while frozen-history injection diagnostics support fact utility. Together, these results support combining agent-level outcome guidance with communication-derived token-level credit. Code is available at https://github.com/Camel-Prince/OPSD4MAS.

title: Visibility-Aware Task and Motion Planning with Task-Centric Perception
author: Sahit Chintalapudi
Xiaoyan Wang
Aryan Zoroufi
Aditya Agarwal
Nancy Kanwisher
TomÃ¡s Lozano-PÃ©rez
Leslie Pack Kaelbling
abstract: Long-horizon manipulation under uncertainty remains a challenging problem in robotics. We present \ourmethod{}, an algorithm for Visibility-Aware Task and Motion Planning. \ourmethod{} extends existing deterministic task and motion planning solvers to partially observable object rearrangement tasks, while still being able to take advantage of the efficiency and compositional generalization over long horizons of the base solver. This extension interleaves sensing actions into a plan skeleton that assumed full observability, and uses a novel persistent object-based memory to fuse observations into object mesh hypotheses and an observed occupancy map. We evaluate \ourmethod{} on real-world tabletop rearrangement tasks which feature heavy occlusion and partial visibility and demonstrate that it outperforms baselines that do not perform active perception or have persistent memory.

title: Guided Generation of Linux Kernel Semantic Patches with Small Local Language Models
author: Mohanned Ahmed
abstract: When a Linux kernel API changes, hundreds of drivers are converted by hand over months, and the earlier conversions are reviewed examples for the later ones. We ask whether small open language models running on a laptop can turn such examples into Coccinelle semantic patches, the rules kernel maintainers already use for tree-wide changes. We adapt guided code generation to this task: the training examples are decomposed by script into a tree of change variants, the model writes one small rule per variant under feedback from applying it to the examples, deterministic components repair SmPL syntax and generalise driver-specific names, rules are composed greedily, and a compile critic repairs or rejects a rule whose output does not build. We evaluate on a pre-registered test set of 7 migrations whose new APIs appeared after the training cutoffs of all three models (Qwen2.5-Coder 7B, Llama 3.1 8B, Gemma 3 4B), with 122 held-out driver conversions, counting a conversion as solved only if the rule's output matches the human fix and compiles. With the framework, Qwen2.5-Coder solves 35.3 conversions on average over three seeds (range 32-41), against 1.0 when prompted directly; Spinfer solves 41 and a frontier LLM agent 66. The local model solves fewer conversions than Spinfer but its rules are the most precise on the test set (0.74 of the files they change are solved, against 0.55 for Spinfer and 0.70 for the frontier agent), and the compile critic removes every output that matches the human fix but does not build. The two general-purpose models stay weak even with guidance (at most 12 solved). All code, prompts, model responses and results are released.

title: WorldDraft: If Code Builds the World, Can Video Models Just Render It?
author: Zhiyu Hou
Wen-Jie Shu
Harold Haodong Chen
Weilin Ruan
Chenfei Liao
Liuzhou Zhang
Disen Lan
Xiaogang Xu
Qi Chen
Ser-Nam Lim
abstract: Multimodal coding agents decouple 4D world construction from visual generation, repurposing video models from world generators toward generative renderers. This division of labor raises a fundamental question: if code builds the world, can video models just render it? A reliable generative renderer hinges on two complementary criteria: (i) world preservation, retaining prescribed 4D kinematics and camera paths; and (ii) visual realization, persistently binding text-specified target attributes over time. To evaluate this capability, we introduce WorldDraft, a benchmark of $432$ strictly paired test cases across $48$ executable 4D world families spanning six dynamic challenge categories. Under a $3 \times 3$ factorial design, WorldDraft orthogonally crosses draft granularity (abstract proxy to previs) and appearance alignment (neutral to conflicting) under identical dynamics. Extensive evaluations across $12$ representative models reveal that: (I) world preservation and visual realization remain in stark operational tension; (II) richer draft scaffolding anchors structure but paradoxically impairs appearance fidelity; and (III) conflicting source cues trigger severe source leakage (up to $64\%$), exposing fragile cross-modal disentanglement. To mitigate these bottlenecks, we propose WorldDraft-Primer, a plug-and-play visual prompting strategy that consistently improves both objectives across frozen video renderers. Together, WorldDraft and WorldDraft-Primer lay a foundation for bridging programmatic 4D simulation with video generation, advancing physically grounded generative rendering.

title: A Coupled Control Barrier Function Approach to Deadlock-Free Multi-Robot Conflict Resolution
author: Gary Rostomyan
Ketan Savla
Petros A. Ioannou
abstract: Many robotic applications involve scenarios where multiple robots interact and the decisions of one robot influence the behavior of others. This paper presents a quadratic programming (QP)-based feedback controller for multi-robot conflict resolution with input constraints. Safety is enforced using coupled Control Barrier Function (CBF), while a yielding matrix encodes how robots influence each other. Unlike existing methods with fixed or hard priorities, the proposed framework enables yielding preferences while guaranteeing deadlock-free operation by design. Sufficient conditions are established for the controller to be locally Lipschitz. The optimal CBF sign- indefinite slack is shown to admit a finite uniform bound, which is compensated through an enlarged CBF safety margin to obtain a forward invariant set contained within the desired safe set. The analysis also identifies an irreducible slack component due to finite maximum deceleration that cannot be eliminated by increasing the slack penalty. Finally, sufficient conditions on the yielding matrix and nominal controller are derived to exclude deadlock states. Simulations demonstrate adaptive coordination across yielding preferences and robustness to robot failures.

title: GC-MoE on SM120: Overlapping Expert-Parallel Token Dispatch with Warp-Level FP8xFP4 Block-Scaled MMA on Consumer Blackwell
author: Yong Li
Haoyu Wang
Kan Liu
Tao Lan
abstract: Expert-parallel Mixture-of-Experts decoding is latency bound: each layer serializes a token exchange, a grouped GEMM over routed experts, and a combine, while only a few tokens per rank are in flight. Prior GC-MoE fused these phases into one persistent, Green-Context-partitioned CUDA Graph on Hopper (SM90) and datacenter Blackwell (SM100). This paper rebuilds the operator for SM120 (compute capability 12.0, e.g. RTX PRO 5000) over PCIe. SM120 exposes block-scaled tensor cores only through warp-level http://mma.sync.aligned.kind::mxf8f6f4: no tensor memory, no two-CTA MMA, no cluster multicast. We rebuild the kernel around a swap-AB warp-level block-scaled MMA with FP4 weights in the register A operand and FP8 activations in B, plus SM120-specific mechanisms: scale-byte selection through MMA immediates, a compact-weights path, an adaptive token-tile geometry, an expert-granular streaming dispatch with a batched bulk-pull engine and a 64-bit deduplicating pull cache, full-width BF16 returns drained by resident relay copiers over a position-major arena, and shared experts folded into the compute role. On 8xRTX PRO 5000 over PCIe the operator is 1.522x and 1.387x faster than the FlashInfer CuTe DSL W4A8 MegaMoE and the Cake MegaMoE across 18 decode points (18/18 wins each), and 1.388x faster than Cake with shared experts fused; all 94 numerical cases and 752 per-rank checks pass, at cross-operator cosine similarity of at least 0.9999997.

title: BWM-Forge: Agentic World Programming for Embodied Intelligence
author: BWM Team
abstract: Generating diverse robot videos requires control over scene geometry, robot motion, and viewpoints. End-to-end video generation offers limited direct access to these variables, making targeted edits and reuse across tasks difficult. We present BWM-Forge, a code-driven framework for controllable video generation in robotics. Given robot assets and a task description, the framework accepts an initial image, an image with motion data, or a human demonstration video. A coding agent constructs editable Blender scene programs that specify objects, robot motion, and cameras. The resulting proxy videos provide structural and motion references for a video generation model, which adds visual detail. A multi-agent harness coordinates input processing, scene construction, review, and rendering. Automated evaluation and user feedback support iterative refinement, while an experience repository stores and retrieves reusable modeling and rendering rules. This design supports multiple robot embodiments, synchronized viewpoints, and appearance variation from a shared scene program. We evaluate the framework on 15 tasks covering five robot types. Compared with LingBot-World Base Cam on these tasks, BWM-Forge achieves higher aesthetic quality, imaging quality, subject and background consistency, motion smoothness, and RoboJudge-9B physical adherence and instruction alignment scores. The baseline scores higher in dynamic degree. Qualitative cases illustrate viewpoint control, scene variation, feedback-driven edits, and experience reuse across scenes. These results demonstrate a practical approach to generating controllable robot videos through editable, executable scene representations.

title: Disentangled Embedding Optimization for Diffusion-Based Dataset Distillation
author: Hongcheng Li
Yucan Zhou
Yibin Wang
Xiaoyan Gu
Bo Li
Weiping Wang
abstract: Dataset distillation aims to compress large-scale datasets into compact synthetic subsets that enable efficient model training with comparable performance to the original data. Recent advances show that diffusion models are highly effective for this task due to their strong generative capability. Existing diffusion-based approaches typically perform class-wise clustering and use the obtained cluster prototypes as diffusion inputs to generate distilled samples. However, the uniformly distributed original samples in a category inevitably lead to entanglement near cluster boundaries, pulling the cluster prototypes closer and reducing the inter-cluster separation. Consequently, the diffusion model receives overly similar latent inputs, resulting in synthetic data with limited diversity. To address this issue, we propose Disentangled Embedding Optimization (DEO), a simple yet effective framework that replaces static clustering with trainable embeddings. These embeddings are optimized to match the Gaussian statistics (i.e., mean and covariance) of the original data distribution, while a diversity regularizer is designed to encourage separation among these embeddings to improve the intra-class variability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed DEO can generate more diversified and representative distilled data than existing cluster-based diffusion methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance and superior generalization across multiple datasets.

title: Indic-Task Gains and Regressions after Reinforcement Learning
author: Sutanshu Saksena Raj
Daksh Maan
Avinash Benki
Parijat Chatterjee
Pasunuti Prasanjith
Purusharth Malik
abstract: We run reinforcement learning (RL) with GRPO across four environments, starting from a supervised fine-tuned 30B-A3B mixture-of-experts model covering English and eight Indic languages. We compare the model before and after RL across 34 benchmarks in one evaluation campaign. MATH improves by 36.07 points, and most Indic benchmarks also improve. Yet XQuAD-Indic F1 falls 19.32 points as English answers rise from 8.7% to 91.7%; IndicQA falls 8.64, while English XQuAD gains 11.71 F1. A second RL run from the same supervised initialization adds an Indic environment together with language and repetition rewards. Compared with the released model, it improves both passage-answering and instruction-following benchmarks, along with preserving MATH performance. But it loses ground on reasoning and coding benchmarks. Several training choices changed together, so we cannot isolate the effect of any one of the reward terms. Script compliance remains unresolved. Adding a language reward did not ensure use of the requested script. Passage answering and script compliance therefore need direct evaluation, even when other benchmark scores improve.

title: DER Aggregators in Wholesale Electricity Markets: A Hybrid Mean-Field Framework with Endogenous Price Feedback
author: Jun He
Andrew L. Liu
abstract: The rapid growth of distributed energy resources (DERs), including rooftop solar and energy storage, is transforming the grid edge, where customer-side assets increasingly interact with the broader power grid. DER aggregators, entities that coordinate the actions of many small-scale DERs, play a key role in this transformation. This paper presents a hybrid Mean-Field Control (MFC) and Mean-Field Game (MFG) framework for integrating DER aggregators into wholesale electricity markets. Unlike traditional approaches that treat market prices as exogenous, our model captures the feedback between aggregators' collective actions and electricity prices. The MFC component optimizes DER operations within each aggregator, while the MFG models strategic interactions among multiple aggregators. To account for various uncertainties, we incorporate reinforcement learning, which allows aggregators to learn optimal bidding strategies in dynamic market conditions. We prove the existence and uniqueness of a mean-field equilibrium and validate the framework through a case study of the Oahu Island power system. Results show that our approach reduces price volatility and improves market efficiency, offering a scalable and decentralized solution for DER integration in wholesale markets.

title: ATune: Unsupervised Photo Retouching Through Image-Editor Controls
author: Divyanshu Goyal
Gabriel Ruiz
Amir Meisami
abstract: Photo retouching models are trained on pairs of original and retouched photographs, usually edited by experts. Expert edits are costly, so the two main public sets, FiveK and PPR10K, hold only 16,161 originals. Good photographs on their own are far easier to find: commercial stock collections and free ones such as Pixabay and Unsplash hold millions. We learn retouching from them alone: we damage each photograph the way a camera or a careless edit would, which gives a worse and a better version of the same photograph. From these pairs, our model, ATune, learns how 13 measured attributes, such as brightness, contrast and sharpness, should change to raise a photograph's quality. The edit is declarative: ATune sets target values for the attributes, and a simple search adjusts the sliders of an out-of-the-box photo editor until the photograph reaches them. Every edit is a list of slider values a person can read and adjust. The same model can drive any editor that makes those changes; we test RawTherapee and darktable. We train on 10M photographs from a commercial stock collection and test on FiveK, PPR10K and SPAQ. Nine quality judges score every edit, and in a user study 157 human raters made 9,253 choices between our edit and another method's edit of the same photograph. When Claude Opus 5 and GPT-6 Astra edit the same photographs in the same editor, raters prefer our edits to GPT-6 Astra's (54.3%) and rate them even with Claude's (50.5%). We also compare with supervised retouchers on their home ground: NeurOP on FiveK and AdaInt on PPR10K, each trained on that set's own expert edits. Raters chose our edits in 46.3% of those comparisons. ATune, a 54M-parameter model trained without a single expert edit, now matches frontier models at setting an editor's sliders.

title: Fully Explicit Stabilized Runge--Kutta Methods for Allen--Cahn and Cahn--Hilliard Dynamics
author: Zheng Tan
Tariq D. Aslam
Andrea L. Bertozzi
abstract: Stiff phase-field dynamics are typically solved by semi-implicit or fully implicit time discretizations, since the interfacial scales in the Allen--Cahn and Cahn--Hilliard equations impose severe step-size restrictions on standard explicit methods. In this paper, we investigate a different strategy based on stabilized Runge--Kutta solvers, in particular the Runge--Kutta--Legendre (RKL) and Runge--Kutta--Gegenbauer (RKG) families. These schemes possess enlarged stability regions and therefore provide a natural explicit framework for diffusion-dominated gradient flows without requiring implicit solves. For the Allen--Cahn equation, combined with Strang splitting, we establish a maximum principle in 1-dimensional case, and prove energy dissipation in all the dimensions. For the modified energy dissipation analysis, we further introduce two new first-order stabilized schemes of RKL and RKG type and derive a novel eigenvalue estimate for the second-order RKG method. We also conduct extensive numerical experiments with both constant and adaptive time stepping, on regular domains as well as on an L-shaped irregular domain. The numerical results show that stabilized explicit Runge--Kutta methods provide an effective and flexible approach for the numerical simulation of Allen--Cahn and Cahn--Hilliard dynamics while preserving key structural properties. The Python implementation is available at https://github.com/ZT220501/SRK-for-Gradient-Flows.

title: What Can a VLA Learn from the Agent That Calls It? Task-Level Experience Distillation for Embodied Navigation
author: Jinze Tao
Yuxiao Han
Kangkang Dong
Yancong Wei
Xiaojun Zhu
Bokui Chen
Houde Liu
abstract: Navigation agents use a large language model (LLM) planner to call a vision-language-action (VLA) model. Each episode needs the LLM, adding cost and delay. We distill successful agent experience into the VLA instead of distilling the planner. The VLA then navigates alone at test time. Agent sessions are not VLA demonstrations. They include motions driven by planner tools and sub-instructions, along with detours. We present H2E, a task-level experience distillation method that converts these sessions into VLA training data. Every motion becomes a VLA action under the original task instruction, with the resulting poses as targets. H2E masks the loss on steps that move away from the goal. It labels every visited state within 1 m of the goal as a stop. We then update the VLA with low-rank adaptation. The VLA learns to stop at the goal and find goals the base model never reaches. On all 3,189 REVERIE-CE val-unseen episodes, H2E raises the success rate of an 8B VLA from 35.0% to 44.9%.

title: Few-Shot Cross-Subject Neural--Image Retrieval via Stimulus-Anchored Latent Bias Calibration
author: Xizhang Yao
Li Zhang
Gan Huang
Zhen Liang
abstract: In cross-subject neural--image retrieval, comparing the mean of a few stimulus-matched target observations with the global source mean conflates subject-specific representation shifts with stimulus-composition effects. To address this problem, we propose Stimulus-Anchored Latent Bias Calibration (SA-LBC), which estimates the first-order shift under fixed preprocessing and a frozen source-trained representation by averaging residuals between target responses and same-stimulus source-population anchors, then shrinks the correction using source-derived uncertainty. Under uniform sampling without replacement from a finite stimulus population, we derive exact finite-population MSE expressions for the unshrunk anchored and global-mean estimators, including residual--anchor cross-covariance, and establish a necessary and sufficient condition for anchoring to reduce MSE relative to global-mean estimation. In a 10-subject leave-one-subject-out evaluation on THINGS-EEG2, SA-LBC increases mean reciprocal rank (MRR) for the Attention--CLIP ViT-B/32 configuration from 0.1867 without calibration to 0.2013 and 0.2336 with M=2 and M=16 stimulus-level calibration samples, respectively. Across six neural--visual configurations and all calibration budgets, stimulus-matched anchors yield higher MRR than anchors with shuffled stimulus identities, but retrieval gains over no calibration remain representation-dependent. At (M=2), shrinkage improves MRR over the unshrunk anchored estimator in all six configurations, but its effects at larger budgets vary across representations; the relative ranking of translation and orientation corrections also depends on regularization strength. Thus, lower shift-estimation MSE does not guarantee higher retrieval performance. The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/Xizhang-Yao/SA-LBC.

title: Reconstruct What You Can: Distractor-free 4D Gaussian Splatting
author: Joel Julin
Liuyue Xie
Ananya Bal
Mose Sakashita
Koichiro Niinuma
Laszlo A. Jeni
abstract: Dynamic reconstruction from casual video must preserve valid subject motion while suppressing transient occluders, shadows, and volumetric effects. Existing methods either suppress valid motion through static-scene assumptions or model all observations jointly, producing ghosting and unstable geometry. We introduce ReCan-GS, a 4D Gaussian Splatting framework that separates coherent scene content from inconsistent observations. It derives a Jacobian-based deformation-sensitivity score from the learned deformation field, using it as an empirical proxy for reconstruction ambiguity. The score guides separation into dynamic Core Gaussians and per-view Distractor Gaussians, or post-hoc pruning of sensitive Core Gaussians. The same criterion supports removal of spatial occluders, photometric artifacts, and evolving smoke or fog without masks, pretrained segmenters, or medium-specific supervision. Experiments on synthetic and real dynamic scenes and synthetic smoke/fog scenes demonstrate its usefulness across the evaluated distractor regimes.

title: Low Language Transfer Speech-to-Text
author: Husein Zolkepli
abstract: A multilingual speech recogniser has heard much speech in its own languages. We ask how much of that it brings to a language it was never trained on, when it is fine-tuned on the little that language has. We score 28 open multilingual models untouched on Low-Language-TTS, 50 low-resource languages in 11 writing systems, and fine-tune 24 of them on at most 1,000 clips a language, 82 hours in all, with a dev set choosing every epoch. Fine-tuning lowers every model's macro character error rate (CER), by 16.6 to 53.1 points, to 9.5 at best, and a word language model takes three CTC models 1.2 to 1.4 points lower; WER is still 34.4 at best. On the 12 languages that no model lists, every model starts at 46 or worse and the best ends at 11.7. The same architectures from random weights stay 60 points or more behind, so the gain is transfer, and an encoder left untouched already gives a Whisper or Qwen decoder most of what it needs. It is the language, not the corpus: on FLEURS recordings that ours do not share, the median model keeps 79% of its gain. It costs the languages the models knew, 5.7 points of CER on English, Spanish, French and German in the median model. Low-rank adapters on 4% of the weights come within 1.1 points of tuning everything, and on 2 of 3 models forget less. Seq2seq and language-model decoders are done within three to five epochs, while a new CTC head is still improving at twenty or thirty. Data beats epochs: 25 clips a language take Qwen3-ASR 0.6B from 60.9 to 39.3, and at equal clips presented, ten times the data is worth 9.7 points. A model that first learned forty of the languages learns the other ten no faster. On a public Malay benchmark, untouched Whisper large-v3 scores 8.9 when it detects the language and 14.9 when told the clip is Malay, because it then translates the English that speakers mix in; trained on the Scicom telephony dataset it scores 6.0.

title: Label-Efficient Document-Grounded Factuality Detection via Cross-Paraphrastic Invariance Learning
author: Chao Chen
Shanshan Lin
Dongsheng Hong
Sibo Ju
Wenjie Yang
Sihong Xie
Xiangwen Liao
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent claims that are unsupported by a given source document, motivating accurate and efficient document-grounded factuality detection. Existing LLM-based evaluators often require repeated inference and incur high computational cost, whereas compact factuality detectors are efficient at inference time but commonly rely on large labeled or synthetically generated corpora. We propose CPIL (Cross-Paraphrastic Invariance Learning), a two-stage Siamese framework that converts a small labeled set into relational supervision without acquiring additional factuality labels. CPIL constructs positive pairs from distinct label-preserving paraphrastic views of the same document-claim instance and negative pairs from opposite-label examples associated with the same source document. It further introduces quantile-aware semi-hard negative mining, which derives a boundary from the positive-pair similarity distribution and balances informative negatives with broader coverage. In the two-stage training procedure, Stage 1 learns an encoder from these task-aware pairs, and Stage 2 jointly fine-tunes the encoder and a linear classification head for binary factuality prediction. At inference time, CPIL requires no paraphrase generation, pair construction, or Siamese comparison and uses only one encoder-classifier forward pass. On the 11-task LLM-AggreFact benchmark, CPIL-2% and CPIL-3% achieve macro-F1 scores of 81.04 and 81.60 while using only 2-3% of the FactCG-released labeled pool. Both settings outperform all compared compact detectors and two vanilla LLM references. Ablations and sensitivity analyses support the contributions of task-aware pair construction, dynamic negative mining, and multi-pivot paraphrasing.

title: Rectified Looped Transformer
author: Musheng Li
Jiawei Zhang
Ziyuan Liu
Yuantao Gu
abstract: Looped Transformers increase effective depth by repeatedly applying a shared block, offering a parameter-efficient approach to language modeling. However, most existing works directly reuse each loop's output as the next's input, which can lead to hidden-state scale growth and perturbation amplification as recurrence deepens. We propose Rectified Looped Transformer (RLT), which redesigns feedback between loops using an interpolation schedule inspired by flow-based modeling. At each loop, RLT forms the next input by linearly interpolating between the current state and its prediction. Such interpolation distributes state changes across loops, encouraging a smoother trajectory from the initial input to the final output. Theoretical analysis proves that, under appropriate assumptions, RLT keeps state magnitudes uniformly bounded across loops and reduces the worst-case perturbation amplification. We evaluate RLT on language modeling corpora and downstream benchmarks. At matched training and inference depths, RLT consistently achieves lower perplexity than a standard looped Transformer, while exhibiting greater robustness to input perturbations and variance in inference depth. Consistent with the theoretical results, latent trajectory analysis shows that RLT maintains more stable hidden-state norms across loops, which also facilitates extrapolation-based decoding strategies. Notably, RLT achieves these gains without requiring additional trainable parameters or extra recurrent block evaluations, thus providing a simple yet more stable feedback mechanism for looped Transformers.

title: SMIC: Shared Multiscale Input-Reference Conditioning across Transformer Layers for Natural Language Inference
author: Xin Zhang
Victor S. Sheng
abstract: Natural Language Inference models can be sensitive to localized lexical changes. We introduce Shared Multiscale Input-Reference Conditioning (SMIC), which constructs a single input-dependent multiscale reference and reuses it across Transformer layers. Each layer applies its own multiscale transformation to the shared reference and injects the resulting conditioning feature before the attention update. We instantiate SMIC in a token--context Transformer (TCT) and conduct from-scratch comparisons against decoder-based and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) baselines across all three ANLI rounds. TCT-SMIC attains the highest observed ten-seed mean accuracy on all three ANLI rounds. The ablations further support the contribution of SMIC. We evaluate a real-valued Llama-style plug-in and extend deletion/insertion diagnostics to pretrained ModernBERT encoder and Llama decoder models with and without SMIC. Across the evaluated perturbation protocols, TCT-SMIC exhibits comparatively low pooled-attention redistribution and smaller signed accuracy changes. We further establish a finite-sample bound on average subset-mass redistribution in terms of the mean Jensen--Shannon divergence between the restricted and renormalized attention distributions.

title: Robot Navigation and Obstacle Avoidance from Randomly Positioned External Cameras
author: Raul Steinmetz
Jair Augusto Bottega
Ayanori Yorozu
Akihisa Ohya
abstract: We study robot navigation in indoor environments from fixed exocentric cameras (infrastructure-mounted, external to the robot). We show that standard Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), which succeeds with onboard cameras, fails to learn this navigation end-to-end in our setup. This failure results from the perspective mismatch between exocentric observations and egocentric action and goal formulations, which is too complex to resolve from the reward signal alone. To address this, we propose Viewpoint-Invariant Navigation from Exocentric Cameras (VINE). VINE uses an obstacle map estimation network, trained with supervised learning, that takes exocentric images, camera pose, robot pose, and room dimensions as input and produces a viewpoint-invariant obstacle map. This map can be used either by a PPO policy or by a planner such as A*. VINE's map estimation performs better than perspective mapping approaches, handles cameras placed across a wide range of positions and orientations without view-specific tuning, requires only approximate camera pose estimates (noise with a standard deviation of 30cm per axis in x, y, and z and about 20Â° of rotation error on average), is robust to intrinsic variation, and extends to two-camera setups with partial coverage. Despite operating from cameras randomized in position during evaluation, VINE surpasses the navigation success rate of PPO with an onboard camera in simulated environments.

title: Eliciting and Mitigating Specification Satisficing in Coding Agents
author: Ruixin Wang
Tianyi Zhang
abstract: Coding agents often fail to meet all requirements in the task description. In some of these failures, the agent considers an implementation choice that meets a requirement, but later decides to commit to another one that does not meet the requirement for a reason it finds acceptable. We call this specification satisficing.
