Prompts greatly influence the generation process, but existing detectors focus solely on the generated texts --- supervised methods learn from labeled texts only, and zero-shot methods rely on the text's probability distributions --- ignoring the underlying generation process, which limits their robustness in open-world scenarios. We introduce SPADE: Soft Prompts for Ai-text DEtection, a novel framework for detecting AI-generated text that transfers better across datasets. Specifically, we measure the prompt's influence and use it as a discriminative signal. We characterize the prompt's influence by introducing a Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) term that captures how much a prompt explains a text. Based on this quantity, SPADE trains one soft prompt per class to amplify the separation, and predicts the class whose prompt best explains the candidate text. Extensive experiments on several benchmarks against various detectors demonstrate the robustness and effectiveness of our method, achieving state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets.

title: Strong Approximation of Stochastic Burgers Equations with Space-Time White Noise
author: Jianbo Cui
Liying Sun
abstract: In this paper, we establish algebraic strong convergence rates for spectral Galerkin and fully discrete approximations of the stochastic Burgers equation driven by additive space--time white noise. For deterministic initial data in $H^1$, the spectral approximation is shown to be convergent in the spatial supremum norm, uniformly in time and in every finite probability moment, with order arbitrarily close to $1/2$. Furthermore, we prove that an accelerated fully tamed exponential method possesses spatial and temporal strong convergence orders arbitrarily close to $1/2$ and $1/4$ under a CFL condition. The key to our analysis is a polynomial stability estimate for the conservative Burgers flux, which allows us to control the nonlinear error using polynomial moment bounds for the exact and numerical solutions. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first algebraic strong convergence rates on the whole probability space for this equation with additive space--time white noise.

title: Time Flies When You Parallelise: Pareto-efficient Time Series Foundation Models with Linear Recurrences
author: Torben Berndt
Lingyi Yang
Federico Nardi
Yi Heng Lim
AJ Shears
Benjamin Walker
abstract: Time series foundation models have demonstrated strong zero-shot forecasting performance, but computational efficiency remains a central architectural challenge. Temporal self-attention incurs quadratic cost in the number of temporal tokens, while nonlinear recurrent state transitions restrict parallel computation along the temporal dimension. We introduce ci-proto, a family of time series foundation models based on Mamba-3, whose linear state recurrences support chunk-wise parallel-in-time computation during training, and inference costs that scale linearly with sequence length. The architecture alternates recurrent temporal processing with cross-variate attention, supporting multivariate probabilistic forecasting with past-only and future-known covariates. Across fev-bench's 100 forecasting tasks, ci-proto XL sets a new state of the art among time series foundation models. The five ci-proto variants also make up the entire Pareto frontier for mean scaled quantile loss and mean absolute scaled error against both parameter count and median runtime.

title: S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models
author: Kaixiang Wang
Junjie Li
Zhaojiacheng Zhou
Jiong Lou
Jie Li
abstract: Typed System-1 (S1) decision models are increasingly deployed in LLM agents for routing, moderation, and authorization to cut inference cost, yet untrusted context can still manipulate typed outputs and alter execution branches. Unlike autoregressive System-2 (S2) models, S1 interfaces score dynamic rules and options without token-by-token decoding, mismatching attacks targeting text continuation or explicit override commands. We propose S1-Evo, a self-evolving framework tailored to S1's contract-based option competition and margin feedback. S1-Evo perturbs untrusted fields via contract-aware evidence channels to induce \emph{evidence competition} with original task evidence while preserving fact invariance. Offline on seed tasks, it optimizes candidates via feedback search guided by directional margins and re-verification, distilling verified flips into experience cards. At test time, S1-Evo retrieves relevant cards to construct perturbations for unseen tasks. Across four benchmarks and three S1 models, S1-Evo reaches 71.99\% mean ASR and 57.47\% high-confidence ASR on \texttt{jev-1.14}, and causes up to 24.00\% E2E agent violations.

title: A Modulation Strategy for Bidirectional Integrated Onboard and Wireless EV Charging
author: Manveer Aujla
Gavin Feher
Caniggia Viana
abstract: Integrated electric vehicle chargers reduce cost by sharing power conversion hardware between the onboard charger (OBC) and the wireless charger (WC). A previously proposed dual active bridge (DAB)-based OBC/WC shares the rectification stage between the OBC and WC; however, the modulation required to realize its wireless operation has not yet been reported. This paper details a modulation strategy that enables the operation of the integrated OBC/WC topology. Differential-mode operation is used for the OBC, and common-mode operation is used for the WC. In OBC mode, the shared full-bridge produces differential-mode voltage for wired power transfer while ideally generating zero common-mode voltage on the wireless charging path. In WC mode, the same full-bridge produces common-mode voltage for wireless power transfer while ideally generating zero differential-mode voltage on the onboard charging path. The method preserves conventional DAB phase-shift power control and enables bidirectional power transfer in wired and wireless charging modes without additional contactors. Design considerations for the OBC transformer and WC coils are derived based on the resulting square-wave voltage amplitudes. Offline PLECS simulations demonstrate power tracking and decoupled charger operation at $\pm$7.4 kW. Hardware-in-the-loop simulations using a PLECS RT Box and an external Texas Instruments microcontroller further validate the proposed modulation method.

title: Lara Mini Base: Language Diversity as a Resource, Not a Trade-off

Jonathan Hammond

Rowena Elizabeth Hogg
Marta Hontanon Del Olmo
abstract: General-purpose language models are trained mostly on English: over open models we review, at most, non-English pretraining data makes up only a 12% share. Models built for European languages give them far more, but score well below general-purpose models of the same size. A common concern is that, in small models, languages compete for capacity. We present Lara Mini base, a model trained from scratch on 6T tokens in English and 44 other languages, which together cover all 24 official languages of the European Union. As training progresses, the 44 other languages together come to outweigh English. To give these languages enough capacity at low cost, Lara Mini base uses a mixture of experts architecture with 7.2B total and 0.6B active parameters. Among open base models with up to 2B active parameters, it achieves the highest average score across standard English, multilingual, math, and code benchmarks, ahead of models trained on 4 to 6 times as many tokens. Its margin is largest on multilingual benchmarks in the languages it supports and on math benchmarks. It supports contexts of up to 128k tokens. We find that our MoE architecture reduces capacity competition between languages. For a single user on one GPU, without quantization, it generates text at least 1.8 times faster than any model with a higher average score. We release the weights of Lara Mini base under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license. In addition, we will release T-HellaSwag, a higher-quality machine translation of the commonsense reasoning benchmark HellaSwag into 110 language variants.

title: The Value of Thinking: Learning When to Reason in Hybrid Decision Models
author: Zhengxu Yu
Ke Xu
Meng Fang
Haitham Ammar
Weilin Luo
Jun Wang
abstract: Existing adaptive-reasoning methods shorten the explicit reasoning a model writes, or skip it by switching modes; either way the answer is still written out token by token. \emph{Rather than deciding how much to think}, we explore a different paradigm, \emph{zero-or-$T$ thinking}: a single model either answers from the implicit thinking inside one forward pass, generating no token, or performs full autoregressive reasoning at a cost of $T$ tokens when that is worth paying. We realise it in a \emph{hybrid decision model} (HDM), where one frozen backbone serves both modes and a lightweight \emph{self-routing block} chooses between them. The block estimates the \emph{value of thinking}, the utility the slow mode is expected to add over the fast one, from what that implicit thinking has already produced, and the slow mode runs only where that value exceeds a price $\lambda$ set per request. Where no per-decision label exists, as in episodic agentic tasks, we introduce \emph{Calibrated Decision Policy Optimisation} (CDPO), a reinforcement-learning recipe that trains the block from episode-level returns. We evaluate HDM on MMLU-Pro, AGIEval, GPQA-Diamond, JevBench, BANKING77 and MiniWoB. Specifically, on JevBench HDM-4B scores $0.857$ against Jev's $0.851$ ($+0.7\%$) at a median $0.179$\,s against $0.652$ ($-72.5\%$). On the agentic venue MiniWoB HDM-27B cuts token cost by $80.1\%$.

title: Compiling Known Rules into Compact Neural Agents: Weight-Space Programming on Unseen Games
author: Jens Lehmann
abstract: Weight-space programming (WSP) uses language models to construct neural network weights without training. We test whether known game mechanics can be compiled into compact agents that generalise to held-out levels, renderings and start states within a game family. Writers receive simulator source with held-out level data removed for 20 privately authored, unpublished ARC-AGI-3-style game families. With a fixed 57k-parameter recurrent architecture, the strongest writer reaches 56% held-out-level success with feedback, while the four main writers' Python players reach 97-100%. An exploratory free-architecture condition reaches 68-90%. Learning from support-level examples transfers much less well, but these learners lack the source information given to writers. Written networks have a program-like structure: 93% of parameters are zero, and 90% of the rest are small integers or powers of two. NumPy players under comparable computation caps reach 91%, versus the networks' 79%. Training the strongest writer's architectures from scratch yields about 1% success within our budget. Written fixed-network weights are fragile, and standard PPO removes most of their success. Prompts for noise robustness increase tolerance by about four orders of magnitude for two of three writers, but PPO makes larger updates and still removes most success. These results demonstrate rule-to-network compilation in this setting, while showing limited benefits over Python programs and no successful combination with the tested PPO fine-tuning.

title: Primer: An AI Framework for Instructor-Centered Educational Simulation Creation
author: Ethan Mollick
Lilach Mollick
Ben Przystanski
LJ Ciccarelli
Natalie Bach
Laura Zarrow
abstract: Educational simulations are a well-established pedagogical technique that gives learners opportunities to apply knowledge, respond to challenges, and reflect on their performance. High-quality simulations, however, are difficult to build, requiring instructor input, scenario design, character development, scaffolding, technical implementation, and repeated revision. This paper presents Primer, an open-source, LLM-agnostic AI-supported system that helps educators create adaptive educational simulations. Educators contribute their knowledge of the subject, lesson, and students, while generative AI produces responsive variations of practice for students. Primer uses a multi-agent system centered around executing educator's instructional intent through the entire learning experience. We hope that by releasing Primer as an open-source system, including its prompts and GitHub repository, we provide a foundation for development and research on educator-in-the-loop AI authoring, multi-agent educational workflows, and simulation-based pedagogy. Further, by allowing the use of various AI models, including local and open source models, we provide the opportunity for implementation under varied governance regimes. Primer points toward a model of educational AI in which instructors can create locally grounded practice opportunities based on their own materials, goals, examples, and knowledge of students.

title: Skill Adapter: Personalized Modification and Online Routing of General-Purpose Skills
author: Qijia Zhuang
Yanyi Gou
Wenbin Ma
Yuxiang Ren
abstract:
Large language model (LLM) agents use external skills to reuse task procedures and experience with tools. General-purpose skills describe shared execution procedures, while specific tool choices, operating practices, and output requirements vary across users. In long-horizon tasks, subgoals, available inputs, and environmental states change as execution progresses. Agents must select currently applicable skills from an expanding skill pool and prepare candidates for subsequent steps.
We propose Skill Adapter, which enables personalized modification and online routing of general-purpose skills. The system distills local adjustments from user requirements and execution feedback and stores them as Adapters linked to general-purpose skills. The routing agent selects general-purpose skills and applicable Adapters based on the current subtask, execution progress, and environmental feedback, incrementally maintaining a task-level online skill library that the main LLM reads on demand. The system preloads candidates for subsequent nodes and rechecks their applicability once actual inputs are determined. Reinforcement learning optimizes the two types of decisions using modification gains and routing outcomes, respectively.
We evaluate Skill Adapter on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SkillsBench. Compared with SkillRL, it improves task success rates by an average of 11.43 percentage points and reduces mean execution time on all three benchmarks. Skill Adapter retains its performance advantage when the skill pool grows to 1,000 skills.

title: DiffSSMEye: Conditional High-Frequency Eye Movement Synthesis with Structured State-Space Diffusion
author: Kamrul Hasan
Mehedi Hasan Raju
Oleg V. Komogortsev
abstract: Synthesizing high-frequency eye movements requires preserving long-range temporal dependencies and subject-specific oculomotor dynamics. However, methods based on generative adversarial networks (GANs) and variational autoencoders (VAEs) can struggle to preserve these characteristics simultaneously. We introduce DiffSSMEye, a conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model with bidirectional Structured State Space Sequence (S4) layers for generating five-second gaze-velocity sequences at 1,000 Hz. Generation is conditioned on a coarse gaze reference, user identity, and task, where identity and task embeddings are incorporated through feature-wise linear modulation. Identity-preservation, multi-resolution spectral, and integrated-drift losses complement noise prediction to constrain biometric consistency, frequency structure, and displacement error. Subject-disjoint evaluation on GazeBase across seven tasks yields mean real--synthetic embedding cosine similarities of 0.91--0.95. DiffSSMEye also achieves the lowest median spatial errors among these baselines for horizontal and random saccade tasks. These results demonstrate improved spatial accuracy and biometric feature consistency for subject-specific gaze synthesis.

title: Maximizing LLM Utility While Managing LLM Fallibility
author: Ekta U. Samani
Christopher G. Atkeson
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can supply autonomous systems with plans, predictions, and judgments, but these contributions are sometimes wrong. This review asks how a system can maximize an LLM's utility while managing its fallibility. Our answer is to adapt the system's reliance on the LLM as evidence about the LLM's performance accumulates. Systems built from imperfect components, such as noisy sensors and faulty software, have long worked in this way, and the classical methods they use can be applied to LLM-based systems as well. A system can change its reliance on an LLM in several ways, depending on the LLM's role and on the other components in the system. Each change needs an estimate of the LLM's reliability, and the LLM's role and the kind of contribution it makes determine what to estimate. Classical methods from decision theory, estimation, and online learning then turn these estimates into reliance decisions. These decisions can reduce how often LLM errors affect the system. However, some errors matter even when they are rare. An independently verified mechanism can prevent such errors from being executed. Without one, adapting reliance using reliability estimates can still keep their risk within a bound. Studies on adapting reliance on LLMs are emerging but limited, and the reviewed comparisons suggest that adapting reliance can improve system performance.

title: Similar but Not Redundant: Embedding-Gated Refinement for High-Granularity Topic Models
author: Daniel Denley
Robert L. Nicol
Mike J. Chantler
abstract: High-granularity topic modelling extracts hundreds of niche topics from a corpus, yet this regime is rarely studied and is more commonly framed as a failure mode: "over-clustering," in which coherent themes fragment into redundant subtopics. We argue that this framing conflates genuine redundancy with topics that are semantically similar but meaningfully distinct, and that the central challenge in high-granularity modelling is separating the two. Recent post-hoc refinement methods address topic redundancy through either embedding-based similarity thresholding or LLM-guided merging. We show that neither suffices in high-granularity settings and propose embedding-gated iterative merge (EGIM), a hybrid approach that iteratively generates context-rich topic representations, uses embedding similarity to propose candidate merges across the topic space, then applies LLM judgement to accept only genuinely redundant pairs while preserving niche distinctions. Across two patent corpora and one legal corpus, LLM judgement rejects 83% of embedding-identified candidates as non-redundant. EGIM improves discriminability on merged topics by 25-55% over a prior iterative LLM baseline while better preserving the original topic distribution.

title: Your Vision Foundation Model Is Secretly an EEG Foundation Model
author: Guoan Wang
Feng Liu
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models are pretrained on thousands of hours of recordings, yet their frozen features transfer poorly to downstream tasks, and this transfer does not consistently improve with larger models or more pretraining data. We show that a vision foundation model that has never seen EEG is a stronger frozen EEG encoder than these specialized models, once the signals are rendered as images that a vision transformer can read. Our method, SeeEEG, keeps the vision backbone frozen and learns only how EEG is displayed to it. Each channel occupies a dedicated row of patches and is drawn either as a waveform at a fixed gain or as a scalogram whose frequency range spans the patch height, so that task-relevant patterns fall within individual tokens. The montage, filtering, and contrast parameters of this display are initialized from a standard clinical montage and optimized with the task loss through the frozen backbone, which amounts to at most 1,113 trainable parameters per view. We compare SeeEEG with seven EEG foundation models on eight clinical, sleep, affective, and brain-computer interface datasets, with every encoder frozen and paired with identical readout heads. With a frozen DINOv3 ViT-B, SeeEEG outperforms every EEG foundation model in balanced accuracy on all eight datasets and reaches a mean rank of 1.3 in Cohen kappa or AUROC, compared with 2.9 for the strongest baseline, REVE. The learned displays transfer without further optimization to the video encoder V-JEPA 2.1, which outperforms every EEG foundation model on both metrics on six of the eight datasets. Replacing DINOv3 with a randomly initialized ViT-B lowers the score by 15.2 points on average, so the ability to read rendered EEG comes from visual pretraining.

title: Control-Gibbs Distribution: Sampling for Optimal Control and Diverse Actions
author: Shengling Shi
abstract: While conventional optimal control selects an optimal input sequence, probabilistic control assigns probability mass over all possible inputs and exploits a distribution of control sequences. Control distributions help enable exploration, capture diverse solutions, and solve deterministic optimal control problems. This work reviews an important probabilistic model for control distributions, the control-Gibbs distribution, i.e., the Gibbs distribution with an optimal control objective as the energy function. We point out its fundamental role in various probabilistic control frameworks, e.g., maximum entropy control, control-as-inference framework, model predictive path integral control, and energy-based models for control. This provides a model-central perspective to unify these probabilistic control frameworks. We also review the associated extensions of dynamic programming for computing closed-loop control distributions. To sample the control-Gibbs distribution, we consider projected Langevin sampling and develop non-asymptotic guarantees. The guarantees show the dual benefits of sampling the control-Gibbs distribution: obtaining diverse control solutions and solving the deterministic optimal control problem. We provide a numerical example where diverse arm trajectories are sampled from a control-Gibbs distribution.

title: From Delegation to Coordination: Learning Efficient Multi-Agent Deep Research
author: Yuyang Wu
Yang Liu
Zequn Xie
Junjie Wang
Dan Yang
Zehao Tan
Ding-Chu Zhang
Junming Yang
Yue Shen
Jian Wang
Jinjie Gu
abstract: Multi-agent deep-research systems use delegation to parallelize search and keep long tool traces out of the main agent's context. Yet delegation helps only when task allocation and subtask execution are coordinated: the main agent must issue useful subtasks, while subagents must return reliable evidence. Existing training either optimizes only the main agent or broadcasts the same team advantage to all agents, which can reward misleading subagent reports and penalize useful ones. We introduce LEAD-RL (Learning Effective Agent Delegation with Reinforcement Learning), a joint main-agent-subagent training framework with contribution-aware credit assignment. A training-time rubric evaluates the research utility of each subagent report and gates its inherited team advantage, while final-answer correctness remains the only team reward; no token, step, or speedup reward is used. Across five benchmarks and two model families, LEAD-RL improves answer quality. On BrowseComp, it improves accuracy by 2.49 percentage points and reduces critical-path cost by 24.5% over joint training with shared team credit. During validation, accuracy increases by 6.78 points at approximately constant critical-path cost. These results show that contribution-aware credit assignment improves the quality-efficiency trade-off of multi-agent deep research.

title: Infrastructure for Verifiable AI: Where Proof Costs Go and How Hardware Can Help
author: Yihan Xia
Wenxin Xu
Taotao Wang
abstract: Users of artificial intelligence services, including those powered by large language models and other transformer-based models, need assurance that inference and training follow the declared computation without exposing private models or data. Zero-knowledge proofs can provide this assurance, but proof generation remains expensive. Hardware acceleration research often reports gains for individual cryptographic operations, leaving their effect on the full cost of proving neural-network workloads, particularly large transformer models, unclear. We introduce a four-layer framework linking verifiable AI workloads, proof systems, cryptographic kernels and hardware platforms, use it to review the literature, and add original measurements of six provers and seven kernels to identify which costs matter in practice. Our measurements show that the dominant cost changes with the proof system and input length. In low-rank fine-tuning, the cost of opening commitments to fixed model weights remains nearly constant across input lengths from 64 to 2048, while the work associated with intermediate values grows. A 13-billion-parameter fine-tuning configuration exceeds the capacity of a 40-gigabyte graphics processor but completes on an 80-gigabyte device, showing why capacity must be assessed alongside execution time. Our kernel profiling further identifies instruction issue and synchronization limits that a bandwidth-only model misses. We use these findings to assess graphics processors, reconfigurable logic, custom chips and existing artificial intelligence accelerators. The resulting research agenda connects proof-friendly numeric formats, reuse of fixed-weight commitments, heterogeneous execution and shared benchmarks to the measured bottlenecks. Effective acceleration requires selecting hardware and proof-system optimizations around the cost profile of the target workload.

title: [Experiment, Analysis, and Benchmark] How well do LLMs comprehend and design relational database schemata?
author: Sriom Chakrabarti
Sean Bin Yang
Arijit Khan
Sebastian Link
abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for database tasks, yet most work, such as Text2SQL, assumes that the relational schema already exists. We ask whether LLMs can design a schema from natural language requirements (Text2Schema), verbalize an existing schema (Schema2Text), and preserve its structure through a Schema-to-Text-to-Schema round trip. We present SchemaBridge, a benchmark of 902 schemata from three collections, stratified by size and constraint complexity, that scores fidelity separately for tables, attributes, domain (data types and nullability), entity, and referential integrity. Evaluating six open-weight and proprietary LLMs, we find that: (i) human-written requirements under-specify schemata, with no model exceeding 0.27 referential integrity F1; (ii) LLM-generated descriptions carry far more structure when explicitly asked to be complete, raising GPT-5.4-mini's referential F1 on SchemaBench from 0.228 to 0.909, even as BLEU, ROUGE-L, and BERTScore decrease; (iii) controlled experiments show that both constructor and describer choices influence round-trip fidelity under fixed settings; and (iv) masked schema experiments show that structural cues support recovery of keys and relationships, while joint data-type and nullability information is poorly retained through verbalization.
Code and data are available at https://github.com/iamsriom/SchemaBridge

title: Auditing AI peer reviewers: a benchmark on real scientific papers
author: ÃÃ±igo Zubeldia
Boris Bolliet
Francisco Villaescusa-Navarro
Pablo Villanueva-Domingo
Miles Cranmer
abstract: LLM-based peer review is now used at production scale, but its evaluation remains limited. We introduce a benchmark that injects objective, localisable errors of four types (general issues, mathematics, numerics, citations) at three severity levels into real papers and measures each reviewer's detection rate by error type and severity, together with its false-positive rate on clean copies. We also present Skepthical, a multi-agent reviewer that verifies citation-backed claims by retrieving the cited papers, mathematics with computer algebra, and numerical claims with executed code. We apply the benchmark to two corpora of 15 recent arXiv preprints each, one in astrophysics and one in machine learning (ML), injecting a total of 357 errors, and evaluate twelve reviewer systems: six single-LLM reviewers, two Claude Code configurations, three publicly available reviewers, and Skepthical. The choice of model has the largest impact on detection rate: given the same prompt, three frontier LLMs differ by about 50 percentage points in total detection on both corpora. Tools and scaffolding help when they contribute what the model cannot supply on its own. In particular, on astrophysics, Claude Code improves on a single Claude call in mathematics and numerics detection, and enforced citation retrieval gives Skepthical the highest citation error detection rate of all systems by a large margin. This citation lead, however, is not observed on ML, where the models appear to know the literature better and Skepthical's citation detection rate is statistically indistinguishable from that of the best single LLM. False-positive rates are below 10% for most systems, but vary with prompt, model, and scaffolding, with mathematics flags the main source of false positives. The evaluation pipeline, the injected errors, and the adjudication logs are released as a benchmark.

title: Ropedia Xperience 2: A Gold Standard for Scaling Physical AI Environments and Behaviors
author: Hao Li
Fangzhou Hong
Zhaoxi Chen
Hui En Pang
Kairui Hu
Mingze Sun
Runmao Yao
Xinhao Ji
Xiyuan Zheng
Xuanli Chen
Yalun Dai
Yap Kim Hui
Dingwen Zhang
Yuanyuan Gao
Ziang Cao
Cheng Huang Yean
Jackson Peng
Rui Duan
Yaobo Liu
Zetong Wang
Ziwei Liu
abstract: Large foundation models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 have recently been shown to control robots directly from visual observations. They nevertheless remain brittle on long-horizon, contact-rich tasks in real-world environments. Further progress depends on two complementary resources: demonstrations of human behavior that supervise how tasks are performed, and interactive environments in which policies can be rolled out, evaluated, and improved in closed loop. Language models have advanced along well-characterized scaling laws; the corresponding question for physical AI is how capability scales with environments and behaviors, which first requires identifying which data to scale and how to produce and reuse such data continuously. To address this question, we introduce Ropedia Xperience 2, comprising 1,589 released metric-scale 3D scans and a collection of 4,230 egocentric recordings of 74 tasks (131 hours). We further show that each capture can be repurposed for robot learning: scenes are converted into physically interactive simulation environments, human motion is retargeted to whole-body robot trajectories, and additional robot behaviors are obtained through virtual teleoperation and automated long-horizon trajectory generation. We propose this joint capture of environments and behaviors as a gold standard for physical AI data collection, laying a data foundation for establishing scaling laws over environments and behaviors.

title: Discovering Effective Agent Memory Designs through Program Evolution
author: Xinheng Ding
Seyyed Saeid Cheshmi
Ziyang Zhang
Tairan Chen
Wenya Xie
Yu Hou
Rui Zhang
Zirui Liu
abstract: Program evolution provides a promising approach to discover agent memory designs and study the choices underlying their effectiveness. We introduce MAPE, a framework that evolves whole memory programs from minimal seeds through a standardized lifecycle interface and an iterative diagnosis-proposal loop. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval yield an absolute accuracy gain of up to 12% over manually designed baselines at 35% of the serving cost, with further evaluations supporting transfer across serving backbones and benchmarks. Empirical analyses and ablations identify and validate two recurring design patterns: retaining raw conversations as retrievable evidence preserves details omitted from extracted memories, while composing retrieved evidence according to query intent helps the answering model use it effectively. Transplanting the composition module into five existing memory systems improves accuracy across all five. Beyond these patterns, the search objective shapes where computation goes: optimizing serving cost alongside accuracy shifts computation from LLM-based memory construction to selective processing at query time while retaining competitive accuracy. Together, these findings offer empirical lessons for agent memory design. Code is available at https://github.com/ash-ding/MAPE.

title: Reasoning Supervision and Capability Retention in LoRA Domain Adaptation
author: Saleh Ashkboos
Dhruv Desai
Lavinia Ghita
abstract: Fine-tuning foundation models on financial data has a wide range of applications, including identifying event types from news, monitoring risk and compliance language, and answering questions over filings and earnings calls. In this setting, the main challenge is to improve task performance without degrading the generalization capabilities of the model. In this paper, we present an extensive set of ablations for fine-tuning Qwen3-8B with low-rank adaptation (LoRA). We compare three training regimes: (1) response-only LoRA, where the supervised response is the label alone; (2) single-adapter reasoning, where reasoning traces from a teacher model are included alongside the labels in the training loss; and (3) dual-adapter composite training, where separate LoRA adapters are trained on traces and labels. Response-only LoRA improves in-domain performance and leaves general capabilities near those of the frozen model. The in-domain change is largest for calibration and argmax accuracy. Under single-adapter reasoning, the in-domain metrics remain behind those of the response-only regime, while MMLU-Pro can rise slightly and the other retention benchmarks stay within ordinary variation. Dual-adapter composite training remains on the same side of this comparison and yields no further gain. Finally, we compress the teacher traces by summarizing them before training, and show that shorter summaries move calibration toward the response-only regime without reaching it.

title: Partition of Unity Data-driven Finite Element Method for Anisotropic Diffusion in Magnetized Plasmas
author: Siu Wun Cheung
Youngsoo Choi
abstract: Numerical simulation of transport processes in magnetized plasmas is characterized by extreme anisotropy, where diffusion along magnetic field lines can be many orders of magnitude larger than in the perpendicular direction. This anisotropy leads to thin, steep boundary layers and numerical pollution that standard finite element methods struggle to resolve without prohibitive mesh refinement. In this paper, we introduce the Partition of Unity Data-Driven Finite Element Method (PU-DDFEM), a data-driven local model reduction approach, for anisotropic diffusion. The method utilizes a bottom-up construction to enable a complete offline-online splitting. We parametrize the local magnetic field and boundary conditions to generate a snapshot space that captures the essential physics of plasma confinement. Dominant modes are extracted via a local spectral problem to identify representative features. These modes are then mapped to the global domain using a partition of unity to form a conforming approximation space. This ensures that the basis functions are fully reusable across different global magnetic configurations, significantly reducing the online computational overhead for large-scale plasma simulations.

title: FlinkEval: A Synthetic Corpus for Evaluating Natural Language Interfaces to Streaming SQL
author: Alfio Massimiliano Gliozzo
Nandana Mihindukulasooriya
Gaetano Rossiello
Erick Lee
Lisa Amini
abstract: Existing natural-language-to-SQL benchmarks primarily evaluate queries over bounded relational data, leaving streaming semantics underexplored. We introduce FlinkEval, an execution-grounded synthetic benchmark comprising 3,903 question--SQL pairs across 45 industry domains and 45 semantic labels. We create diverse schemas and domain-plausible, temporally consistent data through iterative generation and validation. SQL patterns collected from the human-written NL2SQL pairs and vendor documentation drive quota-balanced generation, and execution with a repair loop on Confluent Cloud Apache Flink produces reference queries covering windowing, temporal joins, pattern matching, nested types, and data manipulation. The corpus includes paired schema-explicit and business-language requests, with annotations for analysis by query pattern, complexity, and execution mode. A seven-level Question Specification Ladder examines semantics-preserving reformulation and underspecified requests augmented with oracle-derived clues. Baseline evaluations combine execution outcomes with adjudicated LLM judgments, revealing challenges in pattern composition and request specification.

title: Broadcast, Don't Replicate: Eliminating Weight HBM in Datacenter LLM Serving
author: Hannah Atmer
Yuan Yao
Thiemo Voigt
Stefanos Kaxiras
abstract:
Large language model (LLM) inference at datacenter scale is fundamentally bottlenecked by memory capacity and bandwidth limits. Because model weights are read-only and identical across instances, conventional architectures that replicate these parameters across the local DRAM of tens of thousands of accelerators incur massive capital expenditures, significant static power dissipation, and redundant memory-fetch energy. A recent proposal to use optical fiber loops as delay-line memory alleviates these issues, but its recirculating loop must hold the whole model: loop length grows with model size, slack is fixed when the ring is built, and the layouts that serve modern Mixture of Experts (MoE) models efficiently do not fit in it.
We propose Optical Broadcast Memory (OBM), an open-ended hierarchical Tap-and-Amplify fiber architecture that generalizes and replaces the optical ring paradigm. A centralized memory server continuously broadcasts weights to distributed inference nodes that passively tap the data stream using receive-only co-packaged optics, delivering parameters directly to compute units without intermediate buffering. To overcome the limitations of continuous weight streaming, we use dynamically-sized slack to accommodate large and variable context lengths. We show how removing the restrictions of the optical ring allows OBM to efficiently serve MoE models. Evaluated at a datacenter scale of 80,000 accelerators, OBM eliminates petabytes of HBM while being competitive or better in throughput and energy per token than an HBM-based system.

title: Joint Null-Space Projection for Data-Free Model Merging
author: Tian Xia
abstract: Merging independently fine-tuned checkpoints into a single multi-task model requires no data, no labels, and no gradient steps. In practice the task vectors of different tasks interfere, and the standard remedies--averaging, magnitude pruning, sign election--operate entry by entry, ignoring that each delta induces a low-dimensional update on the hidden features it acts upon. We recast merging as a subspace interference problem. For every two-dimensional weight tensor we take the top-r right-singular subspace of each task's delta--the input directions along which that task moves the representation most--and remove from each task vector the component lying in the union of the other tasks' subspaces. The resulting Joint Null-Space Projection (JNSP) is closed-form and order-independent, needs no forward pass, and is defined entirely by the checkpoint set. On eight CLIP image-classification tasks JNSP merges ViT-B/16 experts to 89.45% average accuracy without using a single image, 11.88 points above the strongest parameter-wise training-free baseline (TIES-Merging, 77.57%), 14.22 above Task Arithmetic, and 0.98 above WUDI's data-free consensus merge (88.47%). The gain holds across three backbones on the independently trained TALL release (+10.8, +12.6, +9.1 over TIES for ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, ViT-L/14) and replicates there at 89.20%; controls confirm the source--a single shared subspace instead of per-task ones loses 2.9 points, and a sequential variant collapses to 69.6%. On RoBERTa-large the same projection underperforms plain task arithmetic, which we report rather than hide. Code is available at https://github.com.

title: Predicting Ethanol Drinking Status from Nonhuman Primate Liver Histology: A Proof of Concept for Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning in Few-Shot Vision-Language Modeling
author: Amirmohammad Mohammadi
Rupak Khadka
Kathleen A. Grant
Mary Lauren Benton
Joshua Peeples
abstract: Combining vision-language models (VLMs) with parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) offers a promising approach to few-shot whole-slide image (WSI) classification in computational pathology. This study evaluates this approach for predicting ethanol drinking status from nonhuman primate liver histology. Adapters are evaluated against non-PEFT configurations on a subset of the Monkey Alcohol Tissue Research Resource (MATRR). All evaluated PEFT configurations achieve higher mean balanced accuracy than the non-PEFT baselines. For example, in the four-shot setting, attention-based multiple instance learning (ABMIL) alone achieves 43.5% mean balanced accuracy, compared with 78.1% after adding an adapter. Qualitative attention analysis shows that textual pathway adaptations produce localized attention heatmaps, while visual pathway adaptations produce more diffuse ones. A pathologist's review identified similar histological features across adaptations.

title: LazyWeights: Decode-on-Demand Edge LLMs
author: Arnab Sanyal
Gourav Datta
Sandeep P. Chinchali
abstract: Memory decides which LLMs an edge device runs, and how fast: capacity on a $4$ GB Jetson Nano, bandwidth on an $8$ GB Jetson Orin Nano Super. Deployed formats (GPTQ, AWQ, $\texttt{http://llama.cpp}$'s K- and I-quants) spend equal bits on every integer code of a matrix, although the codes are far from uniform. $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ keeps these formats but tunes GPTQ so the codes compress, Huffman-codes them losslessly in interleaved lanes, and decodes them on demand in a small unit between DRAM and L2, so GPU kernels run unchanged and DRAM moves only coded bytes. At $1\%$ and $3.5\%$ perplexity budgets, coded Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B and SmolLM-1.7B are $5.7-31.4\%$ smaller than the best $\texttt{http://llama.cpp}$ format. A bit-exact $0.21$ mm$^2$ ASIC decoder unit ($1$ GHz, $7$ nm) cuts Orin latency and energy per token by up to $36\%$ and $38\%$ ($54\%$ and $44\%$ with prompt-lookup speculation). On the Nano, $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ needs $58-64\%$ less time and $53-57\%$ less energy per token than CPU $\texttt{http://llama.cpp}$, and runs a streamed Mistral-7B 6.6$\times$ faster at $3.89$ bits per weight. A Huffman decoder beats an rANS decoder in rate and area at equal throughput; the ASIC decoder unit runs bit-exact on a Zynq UltraScale+ FPGA (AMD ZCU102).

title: SALA: Semantically Aligned Latent Actions Enable Dual-Axis Scaling of Embodied Foundation Models
author: Jiachun Jin
Zetong Zhou
Haonan Wang
Xiao Yang
Jun Zhu
Zhijie Deng
abstract: Embodied foundation models hinge on diverse robot interaction data, which are costly to collect. Egocentric human videos offer a complementary source of experience, and latent action models (LAMs) provide a popular means of leveraging these videos for policy supervision. Compared with world-action models (WAMs), LAMs can offer greater training efficiency and potentially lower inference costs by avoiding explicit pixel prediction during policy learning and execution. However, most existing LAMs learn latent actions solely through video reconstruction, which can cause their representations to cluster by visual appearance rather than by the underlying actions. As a result, they struggle to align human actions with their robot counterparts. To bridge the gap, we introduce SALA, which emphasizes establishing the semantic correspondence for latent actions. Without requiring paired data, we use the language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarities and supervise cross-embodiment correspondence. Specifically, we translate these similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents, while robot action reconstruction grounds the latent space in control. The resulting shared latent action space provides a unified supervision signal for training an embodied foundation model on both human and robot videos. Notably, latent action supervision enables scaling along two axes: (1) pre-training on increasing amounts of general human video consistently reduces robot action prediction error on downstream tasks, and (2) post-training on increasing amounts of task-specific human video substantially improves real-world robot task success rates.

title: Support-Constrained Offline Policy Improvement for Pediatric ECMO from Limited Clinical Data
author: Fateme Golivand Darvishvand
Saurabh Mathur
Nikhilesh Prabhakar
Michael A. Skinner
Ameet Soni
Neel Shah
Ethan L Sanford
Lakshmi Raman
Sriraam Natarajan
abstract: Managing children on ECMO (Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation) requires balancing short-term physiological stability with the long-term goal of preventing neurological injury. Standard reinforcement learning can propose risky, out-of-distribution actions, while imitation learning is limited to reproducing clinician behavior. We introduce Support-Constrained Fitted Q-Iteration (FQI-SC), an offline reinforcement learning framework that cautiously improves upon expert behavior by restricting optimization to empirically supported state-action pairs and defaulting to the clinician baseline in low-data regions. On 78 pediatric trajectories totaling over 6,000 hours of clinical data, we evaluate our framework using Fitted Q-Evaluation (FQE) and a behavioral disagreement. Additionally, we formalize the performance-safety trade-off by introducing a unified Balance Score ($S(\pi)$). Our empirical evaluation shows that support-constrained policy improves the Balance Score by 38\% relative to FQI, improves estimated value by 1.28 FQE units over imitation learning, and reduces disagreement with clinician actions by 71\% relative to FQI.

title: FORGE: Force-Aware Multi-Granularity Control for Efficient Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
author: Liangjun Xing
Ke Fan
Kailin Li
Bin Wang
Xiaojie Niu
Qingwei Ben
Jiafei Cao
Wei Yao
Yebin Liu
Jingbo Wang
Weinan Zhang
abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated locomotion, balance regulation, and manipulation under frequent contacts, making teleoperated demonstration collection difficult: a practical controller must simultaneously provide precision, stability, and contact awareness. We propose FORGE, a force-aware multi-granularity control system with a coarse-to-fine command space spanning velocity navigation, planar foot placement, wrist-pose tracking, and optional force-conditioning inputs. Policy training requires no full-body human motion trajectories or joint-angle references; deployment consumes only sparse bilateral wrist poses relative to the pelvis, coarse motion commands, and optional desired wrist-load inputs. For sustained contact, FORGE combines a momentum observer with a learned correction trained using simulator contact-force supervision. At deployment, it estimates low-frequency, wrist-equivalent interaction forces from proprioception and reconstructed low-level arm PD torques, without wrist force/torque sensors. A quasi-static virtual-target loop uses this estimate and an optional desired applied-force input to adapt the wrist target. A frozen locomotion prior and asymmetric residual actions stabilize manipulation-induced whole-body corrections. Experiments evaluate unified-control stability, task-space tracking, quasi-static wrist-equivalent force estimation, squeezing forces during sustained contact with a rigid box, and downstream diffusion-policy execution of a squat-and-lift task across payload conditions. Website: https://bb0928.github.io/forge/.

title: Learning Dynamics of the Influencer's Game in Resource Landscapes
author: Mark Lovett Feng Fu
abstract: Across domains as varied as ecology, economics, and online platforms, individuals are incentivized to position themselves within resource-rich strategy spaces. In this work we introduce a new spatial game framework called the influencer's game. Within this new framework players' strategies are represented as positions within a trait space. Players then receive a share of a portion of a resource based on their relative influence at that resource's points traits. For the influencer's game, we show that there is a unique symmetric Nash equilibrium that exists under strict log-concavity of the influence kernel. Using the unique equilibrium we show that the stability of the system depends on the influence kernel's parameters, number of players, and the resource distribution shape. For any dimension we demonstrate a stability threshold that depends on both the scatter and curvature of the players. When this threshold is crossed, the symmetric equilibrium destabilizes and gives way to a variety of bifurcation types; including, specialist clusters, limit cycles, and sub-games that reproduce the larger game's structure. We ground these results using real-world data for resources as a demonstration of the game's application. Finally we extend the game dynamics to use multi-agent reinforcement learning and further show that the predicted bifurcation structure persists under partial observability and discretized strategy spaces. In all, the influencer's game provides a novel framework for predicting when competitive pressure drives convergence versus fragmentation with possible applications across domains.

title: AeroZoo: A Benchmark of Well-Posed Flow Problems for Foundation Models of Aerodynamics
author: Peter Sharpe
Carmelo Gonzales
Corey Adams
Mehdi Ataei
Sanjay Choudhry
abstract: Neural surrogates for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) are trained and ranked on datasets that each vary one design family in one flow domain. Such datasets cannot test the least that an aerodynamic foundation model must do: predict CFD-quality incompressible flow in seconds for new shapes in new enclosures. On DrivAerML, larger models and longer training barely lower Transolver's error; doubling the training cases cuts it by about 12% up to 400 cases, exhausting the dataset. We introduce AeroZoo, a benchmark and training corpus of 3,815 time-mean solutions to the unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) equations with a transition model, across seven geometry families, eight enclosure configurations and Reynolds numbers from $10^3$ to $10^8$. Each sample poses a well-posed PDE problem in the form a solver receives it: the boundary meshes grouped by condition type, the prescribed values and the fluid properties. The 2,816 samples with a stable time mean form the canonical benchmark: two tasks, engineering metrics and 22 frozen splits, disjoint in geometry, that hold out geometry families, enclosures, boundary-condition layouts and Reynolds ranges. On the random split, boundary-condition tokens cut GeoTransolver's median velocity error from 76.9% to 8.4% of the inlet speed in single-seed runs (uniform inlet flow: 11.0%). ISLA, a transformer for boundary-driven PDEs, reaches 5.3% over four seeds, about 4 times the change from a finer mesh. On the same test samples, a held-out geometry family barely changes ISLA's error relative to uniform flow, and a held-out enclosure or boundary-condition layout raises it 2.4 to 9.2 times. The data and the scoring code will be released.

title: Inner Product Regularization for Imitation Learning
author: Benjamin A. Christie
Tianyu Qiu
Amy H. Choi
David Fridovich-Keil
Dylan P. Losey
abstract: Robots that learn from demonstrations should extrapolate their policy despite state perturbations such as sensor noise, scene variation, and compounding errors. One approach to this robustness is regularization. Prior regularizers consider each state on its own and limit how sensitive the policy is to any perturbation at that state. By contrast, we explore how the policy's output shifts when given the same perturbation at different states. Our insight is that, locally, the robot should respond to state perturbations in a consistent manner: e.g., if changing an irrelevant object position does not impact the policy at one state, that same change should not shift the policy output at a nearby state. Applying this insight, we develop inner product regularization (InneR). We show that the inner product on action space induces an inner product on state space through the policy Jacobian (the Fisher information for stochastic policies), and that the null space of this inner product governs which state perturbations have a first-order effect on the policy. By clustering states whose inner products are aligned, averaging the inner products within each cluster, and minimizing the smallest eigenvalues of that average, InneR shapes the learned policy so that nearby states share a common null space. InneR enforces consistent responses to perturbations without limiting policy expressiveness, and can be appended to existing imitation learning pipelines for deterministic or stochastic policies. In simulated experiments, InneR makes learned policies more robust to irrelevant state dimensions and shifts between training and test distributions, whereas norm penalties often perform worse than behavior cloning. On a real robot arm performing three manipulation tasks, InneR raises the average success rate of a diffusion policy from 18% to 57% without additional data.

title: XBot-Omni: An Omni-Modal Model for Embodied Understanding and Interaction
author: Kerui Gu
Xing Fu
Shuoyang Sun
Cheng Peng
Jingru Duan
Huayu Gu
Zhenyu Chen
Jiaxin Huang
Cheng Wen
Rui Zhen
Kairui Chen
Zhihui Peng
Shaoli Huang
abstract: Embodied interaction requires an agent to integrate multimodal perception with verbal and nonverbal behaviors to effectively communicate its intentions, including speech, body motion, and facial expressions. We present XBot-Omni, a Thinker--Talker--Actor architecture that extends the Omni paradigm to robotic modalities, including body motion and facial expressions, with ``X'' representing the extensibility to robotic-specific modalities. The Thinker processes text, images, audio, and video to formulate contextually appropriate responses, which are then realized by the Talker and Actor through speech and coordinated bodily expressions, respectively. In this report, we innovatively introduce the concept of ``Actor'' as a dedicated component for embodied agents: a coordinated, streaming module that leverages the native representations of the Thinker and Talker within an end-to-end pipeline, introducing only modest latency overhead. This unified architecture enables multimodal generation conditioned on omni-modal inputs directly to prevent information loss in staged designs. We comprehensively evaluate XBot-Omni across seven benchmarks, demonstrating strong multimodal understanding capabilities on both general-domain and robot-centric videos, as well as high-quality, natural, and well-coordinated motion generation. Furthermore, our results validate its capability to generate embodied multimodal responses directly from omni inputs, meeting the diverse requirements of embodied interaction. XBot-Omni enables robots not only to perceive the omni world but also to express themselves through speech and bodily behaviors, extending Omni models from conversational interaction to embodied communication in physical environments.

title: UAV-Flow++: A Unified Suite for Benchmarking and Learning Language-Guided UAV Flight
author: Donglin Yang
Xiangyu Wang
Yantong Zhong
Wenhao Zheng
Zihan Ding
Yue Liao
Hongsheng Li
Ke Xu
Si Liu
abstract: Language-guided UAV navigation has largely focused on long-horizon route planning, leaving short-range, object-relative flight maneuvers underexplored. To address this gap, we formulate Flying-on-a-Word (Flow), a task requiring a UAV to convert concise natural-language instruction, egocentric visual observation, and current state dynamics into continuous flight actions. Flow encompasses both primitive motion commands and complex object-interactive behaviors, assessing motion intent comprehension and spatial context grounding. To enable policy learning and closed-loop evaluation, we introduce UAV-Flow, a comprehensive dataset comprising 30,692 expert-piloted real-world trajectories across eight distinct motion categories, alongside 10,109 simulation trajectories in the UAV-Flow-Sim environment equipped with task-specific completion criteria. Furthermore, we develop FlowVLA, which undergoes imitation pretraining on mixed real-sim demonstrations and online post-training via Tail-Aware GRPO (TGRPO). By leveraging group reward distributions, TGRPO effectively reinforces high-reward action sequences. Evaluated on 273 held-out UAV-Flow-Sim episodes, pretrained FlowVLA achieves a mean success rate of 75.58%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 6.72 percentage points, which TGRPO post-training further elevates to 93.16% with superior sample efficiency. Physical UAV experiments demonstrate robust execution of object-relative commands in both indoor and outdoor real-world scenes. Together, Flow establishes a novel benchmark and learning framework for language-conditioned flight maneuvers.

title: Actor, Judge, or Teacher? Understanding Decision Models in Long-Horizon Agents
author: Haochen Liu
Qianhao Zhu
Zixuan Wang
Dingming Li
Tongbo Chen
Peng Qiu
Yingqi Qu
Weiming Lu
Jun Xiao
Yongliang Shen
abstract: Decision models answer a question with a typed output, such as a choice among options with a probability for each, so one model can choose an agent's actions, evaluate actions already taken, or score every action to teach a policy with reinforcement learning. Prior work has studied them mainly as actors, judging their usefulness by how well they act. We ask whether a decision model that acts poorly can still teach well. We compare three decision models and three general LLMs as actors and judges on ALFWorld, and use JEV as a teacher on ALFWorld and WebShop. As actors, all six models are pulled away from a subgoal that must come first by an easier one. As judges that see the whole trajectory, the same models credit the steps toward that subgoal, and asking whether each action helped, rather than whether the task will succeed, separates useful from useless actions. As a teacher, JEV raises a Qwen2.5-1.5B policy over GRPO from 72.8% to 82.9% success on ALFWorld and from 56.8% to 71.4% on WebShop. These results suggest that a poor actor can still teach well, because judging an action after the episode ends reveals the consequences that acting must anticipate. Code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/decision-agents.

title: Parsed, Plausible, Wrong: Output Format Controls Silent Errors in Small-Model Semantic Parsing
author: Umar Ahmed
Maxim Dunaev
Mohammad Nour Al Awad
Sergey Ivanov
Ivan Khodnenko
abstract: A small fine-tuned parser that emits a well-formed but wrong tree fails silently: nothing downstream can tell. We ask whether the output format, a free design choice, controls how often this happens. On the PIZZA ordering benchmark we fine-tune two sub-billion models (Qwen3.5-0.8B and LFM2.5-350M) with LoRA on six lossless encodings of the same target tree, from 44.3 down to 10.9 tokens per order, including two matched-length pairs that vary surface form at fixed length. Across 300 runs (5 training pool sizes, 5 seeds) with a hierarchical bootstrap and Holm correction fixed before the results were read, shortening alone never helps, but writing the target in ordinary words does. The word encoding is the most accurate format on both models (87.5% vs. 85.8% exact match for the native s-expression on Qwen) while emitting 4.1x fewer tokens, and it cuts the silent error rate by 2.3x on Qwen and 1.8x on LFM2, separating at every pool size. Error analysis locates much of the gain in negation. All runs also learn to refuse off-menu input (held out: 95.9-99.0% handled) and to apply in-utterance self-corrections. Strict refusal has a measured price: 2.1-10.1% of real, mostly polite, orders are refused.

title: Generalized Gated Recurrent Neural Networks for Nonlinear System Identification
author: Stefano De Carli
Davide Previtali
Mirko Mazzoleni
Fabio Previdi
abstract: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) networks are the two most widely adopted recurrent neural networks for black-box nonlinear system identification, yet they are invariably treated as mutually exclusive structural choices. To move toward a general framework that inherits the properties of both networks, we introduce the Generalized Gated Recurrent Neural Network (GGRNN), a unified architecture that embeds the exact GRU and LSTM network dynamics through homotopies between their respective gating mechanisms. Each homotopy continuously deforms one mechanism into the other, with a vector of homotopy parameters blending the contribution of the GRU and LSTM counterparts. Since benchmark comparisons report no consistent winner between the two architectures, the gating mechanism best suited to a given system is unlikely to coincide with either endpoint. We thus let each recurrent unit learn its own position along these homotopies, obtaining gating behaviors that neither endpoint can express. We pair the GGRNN with a two-stage training methodology: in Stage 1 we co-train all shared and network-specific parameters in parallel at the GRU and LSTM endpoint architectures, while in Stage 2 we freeze the network parameters and optimize only the homotopy parameters. Experiments on the Wiener-Hammerstein and Nano-Drone benchmarks show improved simulation accuracy over the co-trained GRU and LSTM networks on most output groups, and over the reference black-box baselines in nearly all comparisons.

title: Validation-Guided Prompt Selection for Differential Morphing Attack Detection
author: Raghavendra Ramachandra
Hailin Li
abstract: Differential morphing attack detection (D-MAD) compares a trusted live capture with a document image that may contain a facial morph. We investigate whether labelled validation data can improve a frozen-parameter vision-language evaluator through prompt selection rather than model fine-tuning. Version~1 generates 50 candidate prompts and selects the top-ranked instruction using a security-oriented loss that prioritises missed morph attacks (MACER) while accounting for bona fide classification errors (BSCER), response failures, parse failures, and decision inconsistency. Version~2 recursively revises prompts using aggregate validation feedback. On a subject-disjoint test set of 160 pairs spanning LMA, MIPGAN-2, and PIPE, the selected Version~1 prompt achieves a (19.17\%) morph attack classification error rate (MACER), with (0.00\%) observed bona fide sample classification error rate (BSCER), compared with (70.00\%) MACER for a controlled manual prompt. The paired (50.83) percentage-point difference has a (95\%) subject-bootstrap interval of ([43.33,58.33]). Recursive revision does not surpass the best Generation~0 validation loss; the reported revised descendant obtains (31.67\%) test MACER. All 23 attacks missed by Version~1 are landmark-based (LMA) morphs. Overall, the results show that prompt formulation can substantially influence frozen-parameter VLM-based D-MAD performance, while also highlighting the challenge of recursive prompt refinement under a compact 10-subject validation setting.

title: Maximizing Capacity Utilization of LoRA Adapters for Mitigating the Learning-Forgetting Trade-off
author: Tomohiro Sawada
Kartik Goyal
abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning-forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free RÃ©nyi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of $\lambda=0.01$ lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least $16$ relative to unpenalized LoRA. Mean training perplexity improves or increases by at most $0.02$ in all but one model-rank comparison. Single-task and scheduling experiments further show that the balance between learning and retention depends on the configuration. We also observe that several LoRA variants in the literature also suffer from the identified capacity issue, and our approach provides a complementary axis of improvement to LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These results suggest that effective rank is not only a post-hoc diagnostic of adapter quality, but a trainable objective for improving the learning-forgetting frontier. Our code is available at https://github.com/tomohiro-sawada/lora-capacity-utilization

title: eDMD: Endpoint Distribution Matching for Few-Step Diffusion Distillation
author: Tong Zhao
Xianfang Zeng
Yucheng Han
Ruoyu Wang
Mingkun Lei
Gang Yu
Chi Zhang
abstract: Distribution matching distillation (DMD) has emerged as a leading paradigm for distilling diffusion models into few-step students, where an auxiliary fake score model tracks the student's distribution and the discrepancy between the teacher and fake predictions drives the student toward the teacher. In multi-step distillation, although only the student's final output is delivered, existing methods train the fake model on intermediate states or across all denoising steps. Consequently, the student's update signal becomes entangled with intermediate distributions, which can distort the matching direction and remain nonzero even after the student's final outputs already match the teacher distribution. To resolve this mismatch, we propose Endpoint Distribution Matching Distillation (eDMD), which trains a single shared fake model exclusively on the student's final outputs and uses it to correct every denoising step. Our theoretical analysis proves that this endpoint reference guarantees that the distribution matching term vanishes if and only if the student's final output distribution matches the teacher's, regardless of intermediate distributions. Beyond the fake reference, we further strengthen teacher supervision through a precise teacher (PT) that replaces single-step guided predictions with short multi-step trajectories on the final noise interval, paired with a calibrated query density for intermediate steps. Experiments on SD3-Medium, FLUX.2-klein (4B and 9B), and Qwen-Image-2.1 demonstrate that eDMD consistently outperforms existing distribution matching methods for 4-step generation.

title: PACER: GPU Excursion Management for ML Workloads
author: Rutwik Jain
Nathaniel Morris
Yiwei Jiang
Shidhartha Das
Gary Kao
Indrani Paul
Shivaram Venkataraman
Srilatha Manne
Matthew D. Sinclair
abstract:
Variability is an inherent characteristic of modern GPU systems, arising from a combination of process variation, dynamic environmental conditions, and power management decisions. Prior work has characterized inter-GPU variability and found consistent performance differences across GPUs. However, we observe that modern workloads, particularly large language models (LLMs), exhibit significant intra-GPU variability. Their short-running kernels interact poorly with the coarse granularity of dynamic power management mechanisms, leading to unpredictable performance.
A key source of this intra-GPU transient variability is power excursions, also referred to as electrical design power peaks (EDP$_{p}$), where power temporarily exceeds the GPU's rated power limits. While power management mechanisms are designed to ensure reliable operation despite the presence of EDP$_{p}$ sustained power peaks cause throttling that detrimentally impacts overall application performance. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to characterize the magnitude and frequency of EDP$_{p}$, showing that frequent, significant power overshoots are especially common in ML workloads, which combine high power draw, short kernels, and rapidly changing compute demands. To address this, we design and leverage hardware and firmware mechanisms to provide consistent power management behavior that reduces intra-GPU variability due to EDP$_{p}$ and improves overall performance. We evaluate our techniques across a range of popular workloads. Our approach improves performance by 3-12% over state-of-the-art GPU power management and comes within 3% of an oracular solution.

title: Collaborative Task Allocation for Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Systems Through Iterative Clustering
author: David R. Martin
Brooks A. Butler
Scott Nivison
Magnus Egerstedt
Mohammad Abdullah Al Faruque
Pramod Khargonekar
abstract: Multi-robot systems face the challenge of efficiently allocating teams of heterogeneous robots to tasks. The task allocation problem is complicated by collaborative interactions between robots where teams of robots develop emergent capabilities that enable them to complete tasks that would be inefficient or impossible for individual robots. To address these challenges, we present an iterative clustering algorithm for collaborative task allocation in heterogeneous multi-robot systems. This approach partitions the computationally intractable global optimization problem into smaller, tractable subproblems by iteratively forming clusters of robots and tasks, then optimizing assignments within each cluster. By ensuring robots remain clustered with their currently assigned tasks, we guarantee monotonic improvement in overall utility with each iteration. We analyze the convergence of the algorithm and characterize how cluster size constraints determine which suboptimal assignments could trap the algorithm. In simulation, iterative clustering consistently outperforms simulated annealing, and a group-based auction in both computation time and solution quality, and outperforms a hedonic game approach in solution quality.

title: Scalable Conversational Assessment: Chat-Based Exams with a Two-Agent LLM Pipeline
author: Geoffrey Challen
Craig Zilles
abstract: Oral exams are compelling because (1) students can be asked to provide their reasoning for an answer and (2) their interactive nature permits follow-up questions to resolve ambiguous answers. But oral exams scale poorly. In this paper, we present scalable conversational assessment, an LLM-based system that conducts interactive text-based conversations with students to assess their ability to make and support an argument. We use a two-agent architecture to separate concerns and reduce the likelihood that answers are leaked to the student: the interviewer interacts directly with the student, but only receives guidance about the next question to ask the student; the hidden evaluator knows the goals of the whole activity, tracks the student's progress using a rubric, and guides the interviewer on when to follow-up on the current question or proceed to the next question. The system was first tested using a collection of simulated students with LLM personas of a particular ability level or adversarial tactic (e.g., answer-extractors, prompt-injectors, confident fabricators). A novel element of this evaluation was that it required the use of a fictional assessment topic to prevent personas that shouldn't have information from using knowledge present in the LLM's pre-training. The system was also deployed in a small, elective AI literacy course in both formative and summative contexts. Through manual and post-facto AI review of the transcripts we identified opportunities to improve the follow-up question generation and ensure that grading only credited ideas that the student (and not the interviewer) contributed.

title: Sheaf-Inspired Structured Scoring Extensions of LightGCN for Collaborative Filtering
author: Ksenia Belkovskaya
Timur Lidzhiev
Maria Stebliy
Alexander Tarakanov
abstract: Graph-based collaborative filtering learns user and item representations by propagating embeddings over a user--item interaction graph. We investigate a modular, sheaf-inspired scoring extension placed on top of a three-layer LightGCN backbone. The motivation comes from cellular sheaves, where local vector spaces are related by linear restriction maps; here, this idea motivates structured, pair-dependent transformations of user and item embeddings rather than a change to graph propagation. We compare the identity inner-product scorer, diagonal, rank-one low-rank, and full matrix residual scorers, and a parameter-matched residual MLP baseline (\texttt{mlp\_full}) on Amazon-Book, Gowalla, MovieLens-1M, and Yelp2018. We report ranking quality and catalog coverage at cutoffs 10 and 20. The selected structured variants show modest, dataset-dependent changes in ranking quality and sometimes substantial changes in coverage. Our method is inspired by sheaf geometry but does not construct a cellular sheaf or implement sheaf-Laplacian diffusion; the experiments therefore do not establish a causal benefit from sheaf geometry itself.

title: Al-Ghasali: A Computational Framework for Simulating Islamic Jurisprudential Rulings via Finite State Automata and Large Language Models
author: Elnaserledinellah Mahmoud Abdelwahab
abstract: This paper presents Al Ghasali, a computational framework designed to formalize and simulate Islamic jurisprudential (Fiqh) rulings. Building upon recent set theoretic formalizations of al sabr wa al Taqsim that extract minimal operational rules as simple Horn clause logical programs, this work proves that the semantics of closed Fiqh chapters collapse completely to deterministic Finite State Automata (FSA). We establish a formal computational hierarchy, demonstrating that restricting formalization to finite propositional Horn theories guarantees decidability and constant time (O(1)) verdict extraction after offline compilation. The framework formally proves that hierarchical compositions of sub-chapter FSAs preserve this O(1) complexity, and that temporal juristic requirements, such as Tartib (order), are deterministically flattened into static ontological states, preserving the memoryless property of the automaton. To generate human-readable juristic summaries, Al Ghasali incorporates Large Language Models (LLMs) via an architecture where the deterministic FSA strictly controls the probabilistic LLM. Crucially, the paper formulates sufficient design safety conditions for this FSA LLM integration, ensuring strict adherence to the epistemological boundaries of Usul al Fiqh. To neutralize the risk of LLM hallucination, the system employs a Grammar Guided Constrained Decoding mechanism. We formally define the mapping function that dynamically constructs unambiguous right linear grammars from the FSA execution history. The paper mathematically proves that this architecture, augmented by a Bounded Neutral Lexicon and Valence Locking, guarantees the absolute absence of Decisional Hallucination, Juristic Factual Hallucination, and Semantic Inversion reducing the LLM to a pure linguistic transformer of deterministic juristic facts

title: HEIR: Harness Egocentric Intent for Human-Robot Interactions
author: Yichi Zhang
Bo Wang
Zhenghan Zhu
Yutong Han
Jiayin Zou
Gao Kejun
Chang Liu
Shaoxuan Xie
Chi Zhang
Shi Haoyang
Zongxuan Lai
Sen Cui
Guocai Yao
Miao Liu
abstract: For robots to assist, serve, and collaborate with humans, they must not only interpret human requests conveyed through language and multimodal intentional cues, but also execute long-horizon tasks that interleave navigation and manipulation. In this paper, we introduce HEIR, a resource for studying how to Harness Egocentric Intent for Human-Robot Interaction. HEIR pairs human speech, measured gaze, and egocentric video with robot observations and teleoperated navigation-manipulation trajectories, while each session preserves successive episodes, with each request fulfilled through multiple execution subtasks. The captured data, together with human-authored annotations, support the study of intent grounding, execution planning, and task completion within a unified interaction setting. To demonstrate the value of HEIR, we conduct extensive offline experiments to evaluate how models benefit from additional human-centric context across these tasks, together with real-robot experiments that assess execution task completion. HEIR thus provides a valuable resource for studying user-centric robot interaction in naturalistic household environments. Our demo and dataset are available online.

title: Objects as Addresses: Instance Binding in Vision Transformer Attention
author: Khalil Sabri
Guillaume-Alexandre Bilodeau
Nicolas Saunier
Wassim Bouachir
abstract: Humans naturally parse visual scenes into coherent individual objects rather than scattered features, a capability cognitive science calls object binding. While recent work shows that pretrained Vision Transformers (ViTs) intrinsically acquire this ability, how native self-attention computations mechanistically keep object instances separate remains unresolved. By studying this across eight pretrained ViTs, we found that instance separation is expressed more strongly in attention routing than in token content: selected query-key relations distinguish individual objects more reliably than value similarity or residual representations. Inside heads, patches belonging to one individual tend to read from a common image region, which we term their attention address. Visually distinct parts of one person share an address, whereas identical duplicated instances receive separate, movable addresses. These shared destinations arise in part because query interactions with the spatial structure of keys direct attention toward consistent regions for one object and elsewhere for another. In DINOv2 and most other backbones we tested, editing this query component at the selected head redirects its attention address toward another individual. Grouping patches by this query component separates same-category instances, reaching .615 FG-ARI versus .289 for the same clustering of final-layer features, which tend to merge them.

title: Ballad: Bandit-Based LLM Routing for Automated Heuristic Discovery
author: Samidha Verma
Ankit Anand
Sayan Ranu
abstract: Modern automated heuristic discovery (AHD) systems increasingly rival hand-crafted heuristics by leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to iteratively mutate and refine solutions. A natural assumption is that more powerful and more expensive models consistently yield better heuristics.
